articles.title: You’re a Real Python Developer Only If...

articles.body_html:
A few months ago, I published You're a Real JavaScript Developer Only If...

It was supposed to be a little post for fun.

You know, just a few things JavaScript developers could laugh about before going back to fighting their bugs 😅

But the community loved it, and the comments made me realize that developers have an incredible talent for turning their daily struggles into comedy.

Then @sylwia-lask published her own take, You're a Real Software Developer Only If… and surprised me how much fun this kind of post can be.

So I kept the fun going.

I published You're a Real TypeScript Developer Only If..., and now I'm back for another round with Python.

Well, Python developers have a very special relationship with whitespace 😂

They also have virtual environments, mysterious package conflicts, notebooks full of experiments, and that script that was supposed to take five minutes, but it became an entire project.

So, Python developers, this one's for you.

You're a real Python developer only if...

🤏🏻 You forgot one tiny indentation

Your code was almost perfect.

Almost.

Then Python reminded you that indentation is not just a formatting preference.

It's the difference between a working program and a confusing afternoon.

📦 You installed a package and broke everything

Everything was working perfectly.

Then you ran:

pip install some-package

Suddenly, another package needs a different version.

Your project has trust issues.

And you're asking what brought you here.

🧪 You created a virtual environment...

...and forgot to activate it.

You installed all your dependencies.

You ran your script.

And Python told you the module doesn't exist.

You installed it again.

Same problem.

Then you realized you were using the wrong environment.

🐼 You imported pandas just to open a CSV file

At first, it was a simple CSV.

A few rows. A few columns. Nothing complicated.

Then you started cleaning the data, filtering records, grouping results, and creating charts.

Three hours later, you're building an entire data analysis pipeline.

And you're having a great time.

🤔 You wrote a list comprehension and felt unstoppable

You started with a simple loop.

Then you discovered list comprehensions.

Now everything looks like this:

squares = [x**2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]

You could have written three lines, but this fits on one.

And that makes it better.

🐞 You used print() to debug everything

You could have used a debugger.

You could have added proper logging.

You could have investigated the issue systematically.

Instead:

print("HERE")
print(user)
print("WHY IS THIS NONE?")

And somehow, you found the bug.

📓 Your Jupyter notebook became a crime scene

You have cells numbered [1], [7], [14], and [39].

Some cells have been run five times.

Others haven't been touched since the day before.

One variable contains the result of an experiment you no longer remember.

And restarting the kernel feels like playing Russian roulette with your entire afternoon.

🧠 You discovered that is and == are not the same thing

You thought they did the same job.

Then someone explained object identity versus equality.

You nodded.

You understood the explanation.

You closed the article.

And six months later, you still pause for a few moments whenever you write one of them.

Just to be safe.

🐛 You caught a bug caused by None

Everything looked reasonable. The function ran. The variable existed.

But you were trying to perform an operation on None.

And the error message was basically Python saying:

"You gave me nothing. What exactly did you expect?"

Fair enough.

🔄 You turned a simple script into a reusable module

You needed to rename a few files.

So you wrote a quick script.

Then you added arguments.

Then error handling.

Then logging.

Then a configuration file.

Then a README.

At some point, you stopped calling it a script.

It's a tool now.

And you're considering publishing it on GitHub.

📚 You read the documentation and still had questions

Python has excellent documentation.

You know this and you appreciate it.

But sometimes you just want to know why a three-line example works in the tutorial and fails in your project.

So you open another tab. Then another.

And somehow, you're reading a discussion about a completely different problem.

That's programming.

🧹 You ran a formatter and discovered how much you needed it

Your code worked.

Your variable names made sense to you.

Your spacing was... creative.

Then you ran Black.

You didn't change the logic.

But you feel more professional already.

🚀 You wrote a Python script that worked locally...

...then discovered the server had a different Python version.

Or a missing dependency.

Or a different environment variable.

Or permissions you didn't know existed.

Your little script was supposed to automate a boring task.

Now you're learning deployment.

Character development comes in many forms.

🧩 You used try/except because you didn't want to see the error

You had an exception.

You didn't understand it.

So you wrote:

try:
    do_the_thing()
except Exception:
    pass

Problem solved!

Well, technically, the error disappeared.

The actual problem is still in the shadows.

And future-you is going to have some questions.

💛 You started learning Python because it looked simple

The syntax was clean.

The examples were easy to follow.

You could write something useful without spending half your day configuring a project.

You thought, "This language is so friendly!"

Then you met asynchronous programming, dependency management, packaging, decorators, and type hints.

Python is still friendly.

It just has a few rooms you haven't explored yet.

☕ You said, "I'll automate this little task"

You were doing something repetitive.

Surely, writing a script would save time.

So you spent two hours automating a task that takes five minutes.

Was it worth it?

Absolutely.

Will you admit how long it took?

Absolutely not.

🐍 The Python Developer Paradox

Here's the funny part.

You can spend an entire afternoon fighting with dependencies, wondering why your notebook has forgotten every variable, or trying to understand an error that looks completely unrelated to your code.

And the next day you open Python again.

Because you know how much you can build with it.

Python always has another interesting project waiting for you.

💬 Your Turn!

Python developers, although this list ended up being longer than I expected, but I know it still is missing some classics.

What's the most "Python developer" thing you've ever done?

Tell me your stories in the comments 😄

Thanks for reading! 🙏🏻
I hope you found this useful ✅

articles.body_html:
TL;DR

  • An enterprise AI gateway sits between your applications (and, increasingly, your agents and employees) and every model provider. It handles routing, failover, budgets, access control, guardrails and audit logs in one place, so you stop rebuilding them in every codebase.
  • Judge an enterprise AI gateway on five things: overhead under real load, governance depth, where it can be deployed, MCP support, and how much of your actual AI traffic it can see.
  • This guide compares the five leading enterprise AI gateways: Bifrost, Kong AI Gateway, Azure API Management, Portkey and LiteLLM.
  • Bifrost is the strongest all-round enterprise AI gateway for teams that want a dedicated, self-hostable gateway with MCP governance and, through Bifrost Edge, coverage of AI tools running on employee laptops. The other four each win in a narrower situation, covered below.
  • Two things changed this year and belong in any procurement conversation: Palo Alto Networks acquired Portkey, and LiteLLM had a PyPI supply chain incident in March.

A couple of years ago, a gateway conversation meant one thing: stop pasting provider keys into config files and get a single invoice. That's still part of the job. But platform teams now get harder questions. Which MCP servers can our agents reach? Who approved them? Why did one team's spend triple in a week? And what is the sales team pasting into the desktop chat app nobody configured?

An enterprise AI gateway is where those answers live, or at least where they should live. The catch is that the category has stretched. Some products are purpose-built LLM gateways, some are classic API gateways with AI policies added on top, and one just got bought by a security vendor. Picking between them on a feature checklist gets you a spreadsheet full of green ticks and no real answer.

Disclosure: Bifrost is built by Maxim AI, which also publishes this blog. Weigh the ranking with that in mind. Each section below says plainly where the alternatives are the better call.

What an enterprise AI gateway actually does

At its core, an AI gateway is a reverse proxy for model traffic. Your apps talk to one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and the gateway translates, routes and retries across providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI.

What turns an AI gateway into an enterprise AI gateway is everything around that proxy: identity (SSO and roles), budgets per team or customer, audit trails you can hand to a compliance officer, deployment inside your own network, and policy that applies the same way whether the caller is a service, an autonomous agent or a person. If you want the longer version of that argument, the LLM Gateway Buyer's Guide walks through the capability matrix in detail.

What to check before you shortlist an enterprise AI gateway

  • Overhead under load. Every request passes through the gateway, so its processing time is added to every model call. It's invisible on a single chat completion and very visible when an agent chains forty calls.
  • Governance depth. Per-team budgets, rate limits, role-based access and audit logs should be enforced at the infrastructure layer, not left to each app team's good intentions.
  • Where it runs. Regulated teams often need in-VPC, on-prem or air-gapped deployment. A gateway that only exists as a hosted service is a non-starter for them.
  • MCP. If agents call tools, the gateway needs to control which servers and tools they can reach, and with whose credentials.
  • Guardrails. PII redaction, secrets detection and prompt injection checks need to run before data reaches a model, with a clear choice between block, redact and log.
  • Coverage. A gateway only governs traffic that reaches it. Ask what happens to the AI tools people install themselves.

Enterprise AI gateways at a glance

If you only have a minute, this is the table to read. Bifrost is the go-to enterprise AI gateway because it covers model calls, MCP tool calls and agent traffic in one gateway, runs entirely inside your own infrastructure, and is the only one here that also reaches the AI tools running on employee laptops, through Bifrost Edge.

Capability Bifrost (our pick) Kong AI Gateway Azure API Management Portkey LiteLLM
Form factor Standalone gateway in Go, single binary Plugins on Kong Gateway or Konnect Policies on Azure API Management Gateway plus hosted platform Python SDK and proxy
Model coverage 10,000+ models, 25+ providers Major hosted and self-hosted providers Azure OpenAI plus other registered backends 1,600+ models 100+ providers
Failover and balancing Weighted routing, retries, fallbacks, adaptive balancing and circuit breakers (Enterprise) Load balancing and semantic routing Backend load balancing Retries, fallbacks, load balancing Routing and fallbacks
Semantic caching Yes (Redis, Qdrant, Weaviate, Pinecone) Yes (plugin) Yes (policies with Redis) Select Enterprise plans Yes (Qdrant, Valkey, Redis)
MCP governance Native MCP gateway, tool filtering, per-user OAuth, Code Mode (up to 92.8% fewer input tokens) AI MCP Proxy and OAuth2 plugins MCP servers inside API Management MCP Gateway MCP gateway
Guardrails Content safety, PII and secrets detection, plus AWS Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety, Google Model Armor, CrowdStrike AIDR and more (Enterprise) Prompt guard plugins Content safety policy Built-in guardrails with PII detection Integrations, some need a license
AI on laptops (desktop, browser, coding agents) Yes, with Bifrost Edge Routed traffic only Routed traffic only Routed traffic only Routed traffic only
Our verdict Best all-round enterprise choice Best if Kong already runs your APIs Best for Azure-only estates Best managed option, especially for Palo Alto shops Best for Python-first teams

The sections below take each gateway in turn, starting with the one we'd pick.

1. Bifrost

Bifrost is an open-source (Apache 2.0) enterprise AI gateway written in Go. It gives you one OpenAI-compatible interface to 10,000+ models across 25+ providers, and the drop-in setup means moving an existing app over is a single base URL change. It ships as one binary, so it runs on a VM, Kubernetes, private cloud or a fully disconnected network, and most teams are live the same day.

Speed is the headline. Bifrost's published benchmarks show about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 requests per second on a single t3.xlarge, with a 100% success rate. In the head-to-head run on AWS EC2 (500 concurrent users, 60-second runs), Bifrost sustained 424 requests per second against 44.84 for LiteLLM, with a P99 latency of 1.68 seconds versus 90.72 seconds.

On the governance side, virtual keys carry budgets and rate limits that can be set per key, team, customer or model. In the Enterprise tier, governance runs off the identity provider you already use (Okta, Microsoft Entra, Keycloak, Zitadel, Auth0, Google Workspace or any OIDC provider), with SCIM 2.0 directory sync, fine-grained RBAC and data access control, and reusable access profiles so platform teams set the rules once. Routing combines weighted load balancing, retries with backoff and automatic fallbacks to another provider, and semantic caching serves stored answers to similar prompts, backed by Redis, Qdrant, Weaviate or Pinecone.

The MCP gateway is where it pulls ahead of most of this list. It governs which MCP servers and tools agents can use, with filtering at the client, request and virtual key level, and per-user OAuth so each person connects under their own account. Its Code Mode has the model write a short script to orchestrate tools instead of loading every tool definition into context, which cuts input token use by up to 92.8% across large tool sets. In a 508-tool run, Code Mode took the cost from $377 to $29 with a 100% task pass rate. The full numbers are in the MCP gateway cost and access control write-up.

Then there's Bifrost Edge, which the other gateways here simply don't have an answer for. Edge runs on macOS, Windows and Linux and routes traffic from desktop chat apps, browser AI, terminal coding agents and the MCP servers they connect to through your Bifrost gateway, after a one-time SSO sign-in. Only AI traffic is routed, and nothing else on the device is inspected. The same virtual keys, budgets and guardrails apply to tools nobody wired up on purpose, with content safety, PII and secrets detection on requests and responses, plus connections to AWS Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety, Google Model Armor, CrowdStrike AIDR, Check Point Guard and others. Admins can allow or block apps and MCP servers centrally, and a denial is enforced on the device, not just flagged in a dashboard. Rollout goes through the device management you already run: Jamf, Intune, Kandji, Omnissa Workspace ONE or JumpCloud.

For regulated teams, the enterprise tier adds clustering (a peer-to-peer cluster with no leader, so an outage one node sees is acted on by all of them), adaptive load balancing with circuit breakers, signed audit logs that can't be altered, secret management through AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager or HashiCorp Vault, and in-VPC, on-prem or air-gapped deployment where no prompts or responses leave your infrastructure. Bifrost is SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, HIPAA and GDPR compliant, and multiple Fortune 500 companies run it in production across financial services, healthcare, technology, pharmaceuticals and defense.

Where to be careful: the enterprise depth (identity-based governance, clustering, adaptive load balancing, guardrail integrations, vault integrations and in-VPC deployment) sits in the paid Enterprise tier, not the open-source core. Edge requires the Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint, so budget for it separately, and it's still offered through early access, so pilot it on a subset of devices before a fleet-wide push.

Best for: Bifrost is built for enterprises running mission-critical AI workloads that require best-in-class performance, scalability, and reliability. It serves as a centralized AI gateway to route, govern, and secure all AI traffic across models and environments with ultra low latency. Bifrost unifies LLM gateway, MCP gateway, and Agents gateway capabilities into a single platform.

Designed for regulated industries and strict enterprise requirements, it supports air-gapped deployments, VPC isolation, and on-prem infrastructure. It provides full control over data, access, and execution, along with robust security, policy enforcement, and governance capabilities.

2. Kong AI Gateway

Kong AI Gateway is what happens when a mature API gateway learns about LLMs. If Kong already fronts your APIs, the pitch writes itself: same control plane, same plugin model, same team on call. The AI layer adds provider routing, token-based rate limiting, prompt guard plugins, semantic caching and semantic routing across models.

MCP arrived with Gateway 3.12 in October 2025. The AI MCP Proxy plugin can expose existing REST APIs as MCP tools or sit in front of an MCP server, with ACLs applied to both tool discovery and tool invocation, and a companion OAuth2 plugin handles authentication for MCP traffic.

The trade-offs are practical ones. Kong's docs list the MCP plugins as part of its AI Gateway Enterprise offering, and the OAuth2 plugin was still labelled tech preview there at the time of writing. And if Kong isn't already in your stack, standing up a full API gateway platform just for LLM traffic is a lot of machinery for the job.

Best for: organizations already standardized on Kong that want AI traffic on the control plane they already run.

3. Azure API Management

For Azure-first companies this is the path of least resistance. Microsoft's AI gateway capabilities aren't a separate product, they're a set of policies on top of API Management. A token limit policy enforces per-consumer quotas (and can count prompt tokens up front so oversized requests never reach the backend), a metrics policy sends token usage to Application Insights, and semantic caching runs on Azure Managed Redis or another RediSearch-compatible cache. LLM backends can be load balanced, and Entra ID handles authentication.

MCP support is real too. You can expose APIs as MCP servers and, per the June 2026 release notes, package them into products to control who gets what.

The costs are portability and tier. Capabilities vary by API Management service tier, everything is configured through policy XML, and the whole design assumes you live in Azure. Multi-cloud or on-prem estates will feel the friction.

Best for: Azure-centric enterprises with an existing API Management investment and security teams that already trust Entra and Azure Monitor.

4. Portkey (now Prisma AIRS AI Gateway)

Portkey made its name as the developer-friendly managed gateway: one API for 1,600+ models, retries, fallbacks, load balancing, guardrails with PII detection, budgets, RBAC and detailed logs. It added an MCP Gateway in January 2026, the core gateway is open source, and deployment options run from SaaS to private cloud, VPC and fully self-hosted. Enterprise plans bring SAML 2.0 SSO and audit logs.

The big news is ownership. Palo Alto Networks announced it would acquire Portkey and closed the deal on May 29, 2026, and the product now appears as the Prisma AIRS AI Gateway. For existing Palo Alto customers that's a neat consolidation, with the gateway sitting next to runtime security and identity tooling. For everyone else it's a fair moment to ask about roadmap and packaging, even though Palo Alto said existing and new Portkey customers will continue to be supported. One more detail: per Portkey's caching docs, semantic caching is limited to select Enterprise plans.

Best for: teams that want a managed, quick-to-adopt gateway, especially those already in the Palo Alto Networks ecosystem.

5. LiteLLM

LiteLLM is where a lot of teams start, for good reason. It's an MIT-licensed Python SDK plus a self-hosted proxy with 100+ providers, virtual keys, budgets, routing and fallbacks, guardrails and an MCP gateway. Semantic caching works with Qdrant, Valkey or Redis, though its docs recommend keeping it to single-shot prompts and away from multi-turn agent traffic. A paid enterprise license adds SCIM, audit logs and some guardrail integrations, and Admin UI SSO is free for up to five users.

Two things to weigh. First, performance: in Bifrost's published benchmarks (AWS EC2, 500 concurrent users, 60-second runs), LiteLLM sustained 44.84 requests per second with a P99 latency of 90.72 seconds, against 424 requests per second and 1.68 seconds for Bifrost. Second, supply chain hygiene. On March 24, 2026, versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were published to PyPI carrying credential-stealing malware after attackers got hold of publishing credentials through a compromised CI/CD pipeline, as NetSPI's write-up describes. The bad versions were pulled. It wasn't a flaw in how the gateway works, and it could have hit any popular package. But a gateway holds every provider key you own, so pin versions and mirror packages internally whichever product you choose.

Best for: Python-heavy teams with moderate traffic that value ecosystem breadth and have the capacity to run and harden a self-hosted service.

Also worth a look

Cloudflare AI Gateway is a solid managed option for teams already on Cloudflare, with caching, rate limiting, dynamic routing, guardrails and DLP integration. It runs on Cloudflare's network, though, so it's not an option if you need self-hosted or in-VPC. OpenRouter suits individual developers and small teams who want broad model access under one bill better than it suits governance-heavy enterprise rollouts.

Enterprise controls and deployment compared

This second table covers what security reviews and procurement tend to ask about when they evaluate an enterprise AI gateway: identity, audit, where the gateway runs and how it's licensed. It's where Bifrost's open-source core with an enterprise tier on top makes the most difference for regulated buyers.

Control Bifrost (our pick) Kong AI Gateway Azure API Management Portkey LiteLLM
SSO and roles Okta, Entra, Keycloak, Zitadel, Auth0, Google Workspace or any OIDC provider, with SCIM 2.0, RBAC and data access control (Enterprise) Kong's existing consumer and identity model Entra ID with Azure RBAC SAML 2.0 SSO and RBAC (Enterprise) Admin UI SSO free for 5 users, license beyond; SCIM with license
Audit trail Signed, tamper-proof audit logs with export to S3, GCS and BigQuery (Enterprise) Kong logging plugins and Konnect analytics Azure Monitor and Application Insights Access rules and audit logs (Enterprise) Audit logs with license
Where it runs Single binary: self-hosted, in-VPC, on-prem, air-gapped, clustered Self-hosted, hybrid or Konnect Azure SaaS, private cloud, VPC or self-hosted Self-hosted (Docker, Kubernetes)
Licensing Apache 2.0 core plus Enterprise tier (14-day free trial); Edge priced per endpoint Open-source core, advanced AI plugins (including MCP) need a license Azure service, capabilities vary by tier Open-source gateway plus enterprise plans MIT plus enterprise license key
Main trade-off Depth sits in the paid tier; Edge needs Enterprise and is in early access Needs Kong in place; MCP OAuth2 in tech preview Azure-centric, policy XML Roadmap now tied to Palo Alto Python overhead and supply chain hygiene

Which AI Gateway Is Right for Your Team

For teams running enterprise AI workloads with multi-provider routing, agent workflows, regulated industry compliance, or high-throughput applications, the open-source Bifrost enterprise AI gateway addresses requirements that Python-based and lighter managed gateways tend to struggle with at scale. The 11 µs overhead, native MCP gateway, hierarchical virtual key governance, and support for air-gapped and VPC deployments make it the strongest production fit where those factors matter.

LiteLLM fits teams with Python-centric stacks and moderate traffic volumes that prioritize ecosystem familiarity. Kong AI Gateway fits organizations that have standardized on Kong for general API management. Azure API Management fits Azure-first estates where API Management is already approved, and Portkey fits teams that want a managed gateway, especially those already in the Palo Alto Networks ecosystem. Cloudflare AI Gateway and OpenRouter fit teams with simpler requirements: managed infrastructure, lighter governance needs, or early-stage workloads that have not yet encountered the scale at which a self-hosted, compiled-language gateway becomes necessary. Teams comparing options across this range will find the LLM Gateway Buyer's Guide a useful reference before finalizing a decision.

Frequently asked questions

What is an enterprise AI gateway?

It's a control layer between AI consumers (applications, agents and employees) and model providers. It routes and retries requests across models, enforces budgets and access rules, applies guardrails, and records everything for audit, usually through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

How is an enterprise AI gateway different from an API gateway?

A classic API gateway counts requests and checks auth. An AI gateway understands tokens, models and prompts: token-based budgets, failover across model vendors, semantic caching keyed on meaning, and per-model cost attribution. The line is blurrier than it used to be, since Kong and Azure API Management have added AI policies on top of their API gateways, while products like Bifrost treat those capabilities as native.

Should we self-host or use a managed enterprise AI gateway?

Self-hosting keeps prompts, keys and logs inside your own boundary and gives you control, in exchange for running the service. Managed options start faster but send traffic through a vendor's network. Regulated and high-volume teams usually end up self-hosted or in-VPC.

Do enterprise AI gateways support MCP?

All five now offer something. Bifrost has a native MCP gateway, Kong uses licensed plugins, Azure API Management exposes and packages MCP servers, Portkey has an MCP Gateway, and LiteLLM added one to its proxy. The differences are in authentication, tool-level access control and token cost, so test those rather than ticking a box.

How much latency does an enterprise AI gateway add?

It depends on the runtime and which features are switched on. Bifrost adds about 11 microseconds of overhead at 5,000 RPS on a single t3.xlarge, as shown in its published benchmarks. Against model latency measured in seconds, that's noise for a single call, but overhead compounds when agents chain many calls.

Can we move off LiteLLM without rewriting code?

Usually yes, since both expose OpenAI-compatible APIs. Bifrost ships drop-in adapters for the LiteLLM SDK, and teams on a LiteLLM proxy can migrate models, keys, teams and users across automatically. The LiteLLM migration guide covers the cutover.

Can an enterprise AI gateway govern employees using ChatGPT or Claude desktop apps?

Only if that traffic reaches it. Standard gateways cover what developers deliberately route through them. Bifrost Edge closes that gap by routing desktop, browser and coding-agent traffic through the gateway so existing policies apply.

Is Bifrost open source, and what does the Enterprise tier add?

The core is open source under Apache 2.0 and free to self-host. The Enterprise tier adds high availability, identity-based governance, guardrail integrations, signed audit logs, vault integrations and in-VPC or air-gapped deployment, with a free 14-day trial. Bifrost Edge requires the Enterprise gateway and is priced per endpoint.

Conclusion

The five gateways in this comparison cover different points on the tradeoff curve between operational simplicity and production depth. For teams where AI is a core infrastructure concern, Bifrost provides the performance baseline, governance model, and enterprise deployment options that production requirements demand. articles.title: ModHeader got pulled from the Chrome Web Store. Here's how to get your profiles back
articles.description: If you opened Chrome recently and ModHeader was gone, or sitting there turned off, you're not alone....
articles.body_html:
If you opened Chrome recently and ModHeader was gone, or sitting there turned off, you're not alone. Microsoft pulled it from Edge Add-ons on July 3, 2026 and Google followed on July 10. Version 7.0.18 shipped a dormant collector for the domains you visit, plus install and update pings to a third-party server (The Hacker News has the details). The collector reportedly never switched on, but the listings are gone either way.

The annoying part: once Chrome turns an extension off, you can't open it, so the Export button is gone too. If you had a dozen profiles with tokens, URL filters and staging headers, that hurts.

Your profiles are still on your disk, though. Chrome keeps every extension's chrome.storage.local in a LevelDB folder under your browser profile, and ModHeader keeps everything under one key called profiles.

Where the folder is

ModHeader's id in the Chrome Web Store was idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj (on Edge Add-ons it was opgbiafapkbbnbnjcdomjaghbckfkglc).

Windows:

%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Local Extension Settings\idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj

macOS:

~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Local Extension Settings/idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj

Linux:

~/.config/google-chrome/Default/Local Extension Settings/idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj

If you use several Chrome profiles, open chrome://version in the one where you had ModHeader and use its "Profile Path" instead of Default. If the folder isn't there, Chrome may have deleted it when it removed the extension, and then there's nothing left to recover. So do this soon, and don't click "Remove" on ModHeader before you have your profiles.

Option 1: a command line tool

Requestly published a small CLI that finds the folder and writes the same JSON file ModHeader's own export would have: npx @requestly/modheader-export-backup. You need Node 20 or newer. The file works with any tool that imports ModHeader JSON.

Option 2: read it in the browser

This is partly why I built Headerwise, a free and open source header editor. Its "Move from ModHeader" page lets you pick that folder and reads the LevelDB files right in the page (I wrote a small LevelDB and snappy reader in TypeScript for it), with nothing uploaded. Headers, URL filters, site, type and method filters, URL replacements and cookie rules come over, and the profile you had selected stays on. Chrome Web Store, source.

Option 3: by hand

If you'd rather not run anything: copy the folder somewhere safe first, then open the copy with any LevelDB viewer and read the value of the profiles key. It's plain JSON.

Whatever you pick

Exports often hold Authorization tokens and session cookies. Treat the file like a password: don't commit it, and rotate anything sensitive you kept in ModHeader if you're not sure what happened to it.

If you used ModHeader in Selenium or Playwright tests, that broke separately: its test package ships a Manifest V2 build that current Chrome won't load. Here's what works now. And if your setup needs something none of these handle, tell me in the comments.

articles.title: Next.js 16 Image: priority Deprecated, quality Now Allowlisted
articles.description: Next.js 16 quietly deprecated Image's priority for preload and restricts quality to an allowlist (default: 75). What breaks, plus a copy-paste cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
Your team ships a product page with a hero image: <Image src={photo} quality={90} priority fill />. It looked right in Next.js 15. You upgrade to 16, run a visual regression pass out of habit, and the hero image is... a little softer. Nothing crashed. No error in the terminal. No red line in CI. The quality={90} prop is still sitting right there in the JSX, doing nothing, and you'd have no way to know unless you happened to run the dev server and read a console warning that most people's eyes skip past.

That's the real story behind two changes Next.js 16 made to next/image: the quality prop is now checked against an allowlist (images.qualities, defaulting to [75]), and the priority prop is deprecated in favor of a new preload prop. Neither one is flashy enough to make a release-notes headline, and neither one throws a build error, which is exactly why they're worth a proper look: this article is written against Next.js 16.4 (verified against the framework's own next/image and next.config.js reference docs, and its source in packages/next/src/shared/lib, in October 2026), and by the end you'll know precisely what changed, why, and how to fix it on purpose instead of by accident.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain what images.qualities does, why it defaults to [75] in Next.js 16, and what happens to a quality value that isn't on the list
  • Predict whether a given quality prop gets silently coerced or causes a hard 400, and why those are two different code paths
  • Migrate priority to preload correctly, and understand why Next.js changed the name rather than the behavior
  • Read the Version History table at the bottom of a Next.js docs page and use it the way this article does
  • Configure images.qualities and preload/loading/fetchPriority together without fighting the framework's own validation

Who this is for

You've used next/image in an App Router project — at minimum, you've written <Image src={...} width={...} height={...} /> and set priority on a hero image at some point. You don't need prior knowledge of the Image Optimization API internals; we build the model from the prop down to the request.

Table of contents

  • The problem: a prop that still compiles but silently does less
  • The mental model: your props pass through a config-aware layer first
  • Walkthrough: the quality allowlist
  • Walkthrough: priority to preload
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet
  • Key takeaways

The problem: a prop that still compiles but silently does less

Here's the Next.js 15 component from the intro, completely ordinary code:

// Works exactly as written on Next.js 15
<Image
  src={photo}
  alt="Studio monitor on a desk"
  fill
  quality={90}
  priority
/>

Upgrade to Next.js 16 with no other changes and two things happen, neither of which raises an error:

  1. quality={90} stops meaning 90. Next.js 16 ships a default images.qualities: [75]. Since 90 isn't on that list, the component silently requests the closest allowed value instead — which, with the default config, is 75. In development you get a console warning. In a production build, there is no warning at all; the image is just a little softer than the designer approved.
  2. priority is marked @deprecated in the type definitions, and the official docs now describe preload as the prop to reach for. Nothing breaks. Nothing tells you at runtime, either — unlike some other deprecated Image props (onLoadingComplete, for instance, logs a warning telling you to switch to onLoad), priority just keeps working, silently, for as long as you keep writing it.

Both changes share the same shape: a prop you set still "works," in the sense that your code compiles and the page renders, while quietly doing something other than what the Next.js 15-era mental model says it does. That's the gap this article closes.

The mental model: your props pass through a config-aware layer first

It's tempting to think of <Image quality={90} priority /> as "pass these two numbers/flags to the <img> tag." It never was that simple, and in Next.js 16 it's explicit: both props go through a validation and normalization layer that consults your next.config.js before anything is requested over the network.

The mental model: <Image>'s props aren't a direct line to the browser. They're inputs to a decision Next.js makes on your behalf, and that decision depends on config you may not have touched. Quality gets snapped to the nearest value your config allows; priority-style loading urgency gets normalized into one signal. In both cases, the component decides what actually leaves your server — your prop is a request, not a guarantee.

Two separate decisions fall out of that model, and they're the two things that changed in 16:

  • What quality number actually gets requested — governed by images.qualities.
  • Whether the image loads eagerly and gets a <link rel="preload"> — governed by priority/preload/loading.

Walkthrough: the quality allowlist

Stage 1 — the default, unconfigured app

With no images config at all, Next.js 16's effective default is:

// next.config.js — this is the IMPLICIT default in Next.js 16, you don't have to write it
module.exports = {
  images: {
    qualities: [75],
  },
}

Key concept: every <Image quality={N}> in your app is now checked against this array. If N isn't in it, Next.js doesn't throw — it picks whichever configured value is numerically closest to N and uses that instead.

Stage 2 — what "closest" actually means

This isn't a vague "rounds to a nice number" — it's a specific, small algorithm, and you can reason about it exactly:

// This is Next.js's own logic (shared/lib/find-closest-quality.ts), reproduced for clarity
function findClosestQuality(quality, configuredQualities) {
  const q = quality || 75
  if (!configuredQualities?.length) return q
  return configuredQualities.reduce(
    (prev, cur) => (Math.abs(cur - q) < Math.abs(prev - q) ? cur : prev),
    configuredQualities[0]
  )
}

findClosestQuality(90, [75])           // → 75 (only option)
findClosestQuality(82, [50, 75, 100])  // → 75 (|82-75|=7 beats |82-100|=18)
findClosestQuality(90, [50, 75, 100])  // → 100 (|90-100|=10 beats |90-75|=15)

Try the exact same function with your own numbers in the playground below — it runs this reduction live, not a simplified stand-in.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Stage 3 — configuring it on purpose

If 75 is too aggressive for a photography-heavy site, widen the allowlist explicitly:

// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  images: {
    qualities: [40, 60, 75, 90, 100],
  },
}

Now quality={90} on a component is requested as 90, exactly, because 90 is on the list. The fix for the regression in the intro isn't "add quality back" — it was never removed — it's "put 90 in images.qualities."

Stage 4 — the two different failure modes

This is the part that trips people up, because there are genuinely two code paths, not one:

  • Through <Image> (the normal path): a disallowed quality is coerced to the closest allowed value. No error, no 4xx — your visitor gets a real image, just at a different quality than you asked for. Development logs a console warning naming the exact value to add to your config; production does not.
  • Through the raw optimization endpoint (GET /_next/image?url=...&w=...&q=90, the kind of URL you'd get by copying a src out of dev tools, or by hand-building a request): the server validates q against the same allowlist and, if it isn't an exact match, returns a 400 Bad Request. There's no "closest value" leniency here, because this endpoint isn't going through your component's props at all — it's a public HTTP surface, and Next.js treats an unlisted quality value the same way it treats a malformed width: a bad request.

So "what happens if the quality isn't allowed" has two honest answers depending on which door you walked through, and both are intentional: the component degrades gracefully for real visitors; the raw endpoint stays strict so the allowlist can't be bypassed by hitting the optimizer directly.

Walkthrough: priority to preload

Stage 1 — what priority always did

priority on <Image> has always done two things together: it stops the image from being treated as lazy-loaded (so the browser doesn't wait to discover it near the viewport), and it has Next.js insert a <link rel="preload"> for it, so the browser's preload scanner can start fetching it before React even renders the <img> tag. That combination is exactly what you want for a Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) candidate — your hero image, the above-the-fold product photo.

Stage 2 — the rename, and why it's a rename and not a behavior change 

// Next.js 15 — still compiles on 16, still works, but the type is now @deprecated
<Image src={hero} alt="…" priority fill />

// Next.js 16 — the documented way forward
<Image src={hero} alt="…" preload fill />

Key concept: for the common case — "this is my LCP image, load it with urgency" — preload is a straight swap for priority. Both disable lazy-loading and both trigger the same preload <link> insertion; Next.js didn't change what the prop does here, it changed what it's called, specifically so the name describes the mechanism (a resource preload) instead of a vague notion of importance. You're not supposed to set both: the component throws "Only preload should be used" if a single <Image> has priority and preload together — but, like the quality-coercion warning, that check only runs while NODE_ENV !== 'production', so it surfaces in next dev, not in a next build/next start production run.

Stage 3 — reaching past preload when you need more control

The docs are explicit that preload isn't always the right tool, even for an above-the-fold image: "In most cases, you should use loading="eager" or fetchPriority="high" instead of preload." Reach for those two directly when:

// Multiple images could plausibly be the LCP element depending on viewport size —
// don't blanket them all with preload (that fights the browser's own prioritization)
<Image src={hero} alt="…" loading="eager" fetchPriority="high" fill />

preload is a blunt, singular signal — "fetch this one early, with a <link> tag." loading/fetchPriority let the browser's own scheduler make the call across several candidates, which matters once a layout has more than one image that could end up being the LCP element on different screen sizes.

Edge cases and gotchas

  • Nothing warns you to migrate priority. It's @deprecated in the types (your editor may gray it out or flag it with a linter that reads JSDoc), but there is no runtime console message pointing you to preload, so code that never gets a type-check pass can carry priority indefinitely without anyone noticing it's the old name.
  • The production quality warning doesn't exist. The images.qualities mismatch warning only fires in development (NODE_ENV !== 'production'). A staging environment running a production build will not tell you a quality prop is being coerced — only next dev will.
  • A static import's quality is checked too. quality behaves identically whether src is a remote URL, a path under public/, or a statically imported image — the allowlist check doesn't care how the src arrived.
  • Raising the allowlist raises optimizer work. Every quality value you add to images.qualities is a value the Image Optimization API may actually have to render on demand. A wide allowlist (say, every integer 1–100) defeats the point of having one at all — the docs frame the default narrow list as a deliberate guard against letting "malicious actors... optimize more qualities than you intended," since each distinct quality is a distinct image variant your server (or your hosting provider's optimizer) has to produce and cache.
  • priority/preload and loading="lazy" are mutually exclusive, and so are priority and preload together. The component throws for either combination rather than silently picking one — but that throw lives in the same NODE_ENV !== 'production'-gated code as the quality warning, so it's a next dev error, not a guarantee your next build/CI pipeline will catch it. If you only ever test with a production build, an invalid combination can ship unnoticed.

Best practices

  • Set images.qualities once, deliberately, in next.config.js, based on the quality values your designs actually use — don't leave it at the 16 default if your app already standardizes on, say, 85 for photography.
  • Reserve preload for the one true LCP candidate on a given page. If more than one image could be it depending on viewport, use loading="eager"/fetchPriority="high" on the candidates instead and let the browser's scanner decide.
  • Run next dev at least once after a major upgrade, specifically to read the console for images.qualities warnings — they don't appear in a production build, and they're the only signal this change produces.
  • Grep for priority across .tsx files during a 15→16 upgrade and rename to preload as a mechanical pass; it's a safe, behavior-preserving rename for the common usage described above.
  • Don't widen images.qualities to "everything" as a reflexive fix — pick the two or three values your design system actually ships, the same way you'd pick deviceSizes.

FAQ

Does quality={90} throw an error in Next.js 16?

No. If 90 isn't in your images.qualities allowlist, the component silently requests the closest allowed value instead (75, with the default config). No exception, no build failure — just a different number than the one in your JSX. The console warning for this only appears in development.

Why does hitting /_next/image?...&q=90 directly return a 400 but the component doesn't error?

Because they're different code paths. The <Image> component coerces an out-of-range quality to the closest allowed value before building the request — it never sends an invalid q. The raw optimizer endpoint validates q as a strict allowlist with no coercion, because it's a public HTTP surface that has to reject bad input rather than guess what you meant.

Is priority removed in Next.js 16?

No, it's deprecated, not removed. It still compiles and still behaves the same as preload for the eager-load-plus-preload-link use case. The Version History table in the official <Image> reference records it as deprecated starting in v16.0.0.

Do I need to migrate priority to preload immediately?

Not urgently — there's no runtime warning pushing you to, and the behavior hasn't changed. Treat it like any other mechanical rename: do it the next time you're already touching a file, or as a dedicated sweep during a major-version upgrade, rather than a hotfix.

Does images.qualities affect images served through a custom loader?

Only partly. The dev-only console warning for an out-of-allowlist quality fires regardless of which loader you use. But the actual snap-to-closest-value coercion (findClosestQuality) is implemented inside Next.js's own default loader, not in a shared layer every loader passes through — a custom loader function or images.loaderFile receives the raw quality prop exactly as written and is responsible for applying (or ignoring) images.qualities itself. It also isn't going through the /_next/image endpoint in the typical case, so the strict-400 behavior doesn't apply there either.

Cheat sheet 

// next.config.js — the Next.js 16 defaults, written out explicitly
module.exports = {
  images: {
    qualities: [75],        // REQUIRED allowlist since v16.0.0; unlisted quality → closest match
  },
}
Task Code What actually happens
Request a quality on the allowlist <Image quality={75} /> Requested exactly as given
Request a quality NOT on the allowlist <Image quality={90} /> (allowlist [75]) Silently coerced to 75 (closest match); dev-only console warning
Widen what's allowed images: { qualities: [50, 75, 100] } quality={90} now resolves to 100 (closest), not 75
Hit the optimizer directly with a bad quality GET /_next/image?url=...&w=640&q=90 (not on allowlist) 400 Bad Request — no coercion on this path
Mark the LCP / hero image (current) <Image preload fill /> Eager load + <link rel="preload"> inserted
Mark the LCP / hero image (deprecated, still works) <Image priority fill /> Identical to preload — no runtime warning to switch
Multiple possible LCP candidates <Image loading="eager" fetchPriority="high" /> Finer-grained signal than preload; lets the browser's scanner weigh several images
Invalid combination (next dev-only error) <Image priority preload /> or <Image priority loading="lazy" /> Throws: "Only preload should be used" / "Only one should be used" — only while NODE_ENV !== 'production'

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 8-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Key takeaways

  • images.qualities defaults to [75] in Next.js 16. Any quality prop not on your configured allowlist is silently snapped to the closest value that is — gracefully through <Image>, strictly (400) through the raw optimizer endpoint.
  • The coercion warning is development-only. A production build will not tell you a quality value got rewritten; the only way to catch it is to run next dev and read the console, or to simply set the allowlist to match your design system up front.
  • priority isn't gone, it's renamed to preload, and for the one thing almost everyone uses it for — flagging the LCP image — the swap is behavior-preserving. Nothing nags you to make it, so plan it as a deliberate pass rather than waiting for a warning that will never come.
  • loading="eager" + fetchPriority="high" is the more precise tool when a page has more than one plausible LCP candidate; preload is for the single, known one.

You upgrade, the build succeeds, the page looks almost right — and that gap between "compiles" and "renders exactly as specified" is where both of these changes live. Now that you've seen the allowlist and the rename from the inside, a soft hero image or a silently-working priority prop stops being a mystery and starts being a one-line fix in next.config.js or a safe find-and-replace.

If you've been caught by either of these since upgrading to Next.js 16, or found a case the allowlist handles differently than described here, say so in the comments — these are the two next/image changes with the fewest search results and the most "wait, why did my image get softer" GitHub issues.

articles.title: Your Tabs Each Open Their Own WebSocket. navigator.locks Elects One.
articles.description: Six open tabs means six live connections to your server, six duplicate pushes, six timers draining the battery. navigator.locks elects a single leader tab to hold the real connection — the rest just listen.
articles.body_html:
Open your app in six tabs — most people have at least that many of something open right now — and check your server's connection count. If you're using WebSockets or Server-Sent Events for live updates, it just went up by six. Six sockets, six keep-alives, six copies of every push notification landing in the same browser window.

Nobody asked for six connections. They asked to see their dashboard update live. You gave them that, and also a server bill and a battery drain that scale with how many tabs a bookmark-happy user happens to have open.

The bug you can see in your own network tab

Open devtools, go to the Network tab, filter by WS, and open the same page twice. You'll see two independent socket connections, each sending its own ping, each receiving its own copy of every broadcast the server sends.

Now open six. Your server — which probably caps concurrent connections per deploy, or bills per connection-minute — just got six times the load from one human being. And when the server pushes a notification, that human sees it pop up six times, once per tab, because each tab's JavaScript has no idea the other five exist.

The fix that doesn't fix it

The obvious instinct is the Page Visibility API: pause the connection in background tabs, since the user is only looking at one of them anyway.

document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => {
  if (document.hidden) socket.close();
  else socket = new WebSocket(url);
});

This helps a little and breaks something else. A user with the dashboard open on a second monitor, in a visible-but-not-active tab, stops getting updates. Worse, "hidden" and "pointless" aren't the same thing — a background tab doing the actual relaying for a visible one is exactly what you want, not what you're trying to kill.

The real problem was never "which tabs should connect." It's that six tabs are duplicating work that only needs to happen once. You don't want fewer connections scattered unpredictably across whichever tabs happen to be visible — you want exactly one connection, owned by exactly one tab, with the other five just listening in.

That's leader election, and the browser already ships the primitive for it.

navigator.locks, held for the life of a tab

navigator.locks.request() normally looks like a mutex: acquire a named lock, do some work, let it resolve, the lock releases. But nothing requires the callback to resolve quickly. Give it a promise that never resolves on its own, and the lock stays held for as long as that tab is open — the moment the tab closes, crashes, or navigates away, the browser releases the lock for you, automatically, no cleanup code required.

That's the whole mechanism. Whichever tab's request() call wins the (exclusive, FIFO) queue becomes the leader. Every other tab's request just waits — and the instant the leader's tab closes, the next one in line is granted the lock and takes over.

const LEADER_LOCK = 'app-connection-leader';
let socket;

navigator.locks.request(LEADER_LOCK, () => {
  // Only one tab's callback ever runs this at a time.
  socket = new WebSocket('wss://example.com/live');
  socket.onmessage = (e) => {
    channel.postMessage({ tick: e.data }); // fan out to every other tab
    renderUpdate(e.data);                  // and render here too — see why below
  };

  return new Promise(() => {}); // never resolves — holds the lock until this tab dies
});

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Relaying to the followers

Electing a leader only solves half the problem — the other five tabs still need the updates. That's what BroadcastChannel is for: the leader relays every message it receives onto a channel that every other tab is already listening to.

const channel = new BroadcastChannel('app-updates');

// Every follower tab runs this:
channel.onmessage = (e) => renderUpdate(e.data.tick);

Here's the gotcha worth knowing before you build this: a BroadcastChannel never delivers a message back to the instance that posted it — that's by design, not a bug. So the leader can't just post to the channel and expect its own onmessage to fire; that's why the leader's socket.onmessage above renders directly instead of waiting for an echo that will never arrive. Followers never touch the real connection — they only ever get updates through the channel. If a follower needs to send something back (a user action, a form submit), it posts that onto the channel too, and the leader is the only one that forwards it to the server. One tab talks to your backend. The rest just listen.

What happens when the leader closes

This is the part worth testing yourself, because it's the part that makes this worth doing at all: close the leader tab, and one of the waiting tabs is granted the lock as soon as the browser notices that tab's context is gone — no polling, no "is anyone still there" timeout, no stale leader lingering for thirty seconds before a new one takes over. The browser's lock queue is the failover mechanism — you don't write one.

There's a brief gap you should know about: the new leader has to open its own WebSocket connection after acquiring the lock, so there's a reconnect delay (normal connection-establishment time) before live updates resume. For a dashboard or notification feed, that's invisible. For something that can't tolerate a gap at all, keep that in mind rather than assuming the handoff is instant.

One more option worth knowing: navigator.locks.request(name, { ifAvailable: true }, callback) checks leadership without joining the queue — callback runs immediately with null if someone else already holds the lock, instead of waiting. Useful for a tab that wants to know "am I the leader?" without volunteering to become one.

Try it with real tabs, not a mental model

Everything above is easy to agree with and easy to get wrong in practice — the FIFO ordering, the automatic release, the reconnect gap. The playground above runs the exact same navigator.locks + BroadcastChannel code in three simulated tabs on one page. Open each one, watch the lock queue hand off leadership the moment you close the leader, and try the "steal" option to see what happens when a tab forces its way to the front instead of waiting in line.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Browser support, honestly

navigator.locks is Baseline widely available — Chrome 69+, Firefox 96+, Safari 15.4+ — so this works in every current browser. The one footgun is the steal option: it forcibly yanks the lock away from whoever holds it, skipping the queue entirely. That's occasionally the right tool (a user force-reloading a stuck tab), but use it knowing the previous leader never gets a chance to finish cleanly — it just loses the lock mid-flight.

You don't need six tabs each holding their own connection to do the job of one. You need one tab doing the job, and a browser API that already knows how to pick which one — and hand the job to the next tab the moment the first one leaves.

Does your app open a connection per tab right now? Go count it in the Network panel — I'll bet it's more than you think.

articles.title: CircleCI’s runners were ready. The database couldn’t tell them what to run.
articles.description: Around 3,500 job starts failed because PostgreSQL’s WAL generation outpaced archival during routine...
articles.body_html:
Around 3,500 job starts failed because PostgreSQL’s WAL generation outpaced archival during routine anti-wraparound autovacuum.

The dedicated log volume filled, and CircleCI’s orchestration database went offline for 50 minutes. A maintenance operation had turned into a developer-feedback outage.

How Routine Vacuum Work Filled the WAL Disk

PostgreSQL autovacuum is routine maintenance, not an optional background nicety. CircleCI's report says an anti-wraparound autovacuum ran on several of its largest tables. On a very large table the process reads every page and produces a large volume of transaction logs. Around 12:40 UTC, this maintenance output plus normal application writes exceeded the rate at which the database could archive and reclaim the dedicated log volume.

The failure was a rate mismatch, not simply a database that had “too little disk.” If WAL is produced at rate g and archived at rate a, free space falls whenever g > a. Disk headroom buys time, but does not correct the mismatch. CircleCI did not publish those rates or the volume size, so the inequality explains the mechanism without pretending to reconstruct its capacity numbers.

Alerts began showing brief orchestration errors at 10:02. They cleared within about 15 minutes and looked similar to alerts responders had seen before. As the WAL volume filled, slowdowns became intermittent around 13:30, then continuous by 15:30. The incident was declared at 14:54. CircleCI's retrospective says the noisy, short-lived alerts and the absence of direct alerts on WAL volume and archive lag delayed recognition of the combined failure.

The more interesting part? Bringing the database back wasn’t enough. The storage change cut processing speed to roughly half its normal rate, and the backlog kept hurting customers for hours. It’s a good reminder that database recovery and service recovery are two very different things.

We broke down the failure mechanism, recovery timeline, architectural bottleneck, and the safeguards worth adding.

Full postmortem: https://buildopsy.com/system-design/circleci-wal-autovacuum-postmortem.html

articles.title: Soft 404s in SaaS Docs: Choose a Real Replacement or a Real Error
articles.description: To fix a soft 404 in SaaS docs, decide whether the guide moved, was retired without a replacement or...
articles.body_html:
To fix a soft 404 in SaaS docs, decide whether the guide moved, was retired without a replacement or is still supposed to work. Then make the HTTP response and the visible page agree with that decision. Redirect a moved guide to its relevant replacement, return a real error for missing content, and repair a live guide that is failing to load.

A soft 404 is a page that appears missing or empty while the server reports success. Google's troubleshooting guide explains these cases and the different repairs. The worked release example below is hypothetical. It is a review method for your documentation team, not a report of changes deployed to an actual site.

Read the response and the body together

Start with the exact URL in the error report. Record its HTTP status, any redirects, final address and visible main content. The status is the server's response to a request. The rendered body is what the visitor sees after the page loads. A success code alone cannot tell you whether the expected guide is present.

For example, an application might display its normal navigation and then say “Guide not found.” The layout looks familiar, but the promised content is missing. If the server returned 200, the message and status disagree. A page can also look nearly blank when a content request fails. Check the actual route rather than assuming the common shell means the document loaded.

Use the team's existing response-inspection tools and inspect the rendered page in a browser. Google also recommends URL Inspection for the response and rendered content in these cases. Save the observation before changing anything. It helps distinguish an intentionally retired guide from a working guide that briefly failed because a resource did not load.

Classify three routes before choosing a fix

Imagine a fictional SaaS documentation release with three affected addresses. Route A is an export guide moved into a new documentation section. Route B explains a retired integration with no equivalent feature. Route C is a current billing guide whose content request is failing. These invented routes represent different content decisions, even if all three look like missing pages during review.

For Route A, first open the proposed replacement. Does it teach the same export task? Are the permission rules and file contents current? If it answers a different question, it is not a good replacement simply because it lives in the same section. A useful destination preserves the reader's reason for following the old link.

For Route B, ask whether an accurate archive is needed. Some teams intentionally keep historical instructions for older supported versions. If that is the plan, the archive needs clear version boundaries and real content. If the integration and its guide are removed with no similar replacement, record that decision. Do not leave an empty page pretending the feature is available.

For Route C, retirement is the wrong diagnosis. The guide is still needed, so inspect the content source, request failure and resources required to render it. A redirect might hide the broken route without restoring the billing answer. Keep the task focused on getting the intended document to load correctly and verifying the public result.

Make the moved guide land on the right answer

Google's troubleshooting guidance recommends a permanent 301 redirect when a page has moved or has a clear replacement. Apply that to the fictional Route A only after verifying the destination. Record the old address, final replacement and reason they are equivalent. This record gives a reviewer something more useful than a list of redirects with no content context.

Then follow the old link as a visitor. Confirm the final URL and read the destination's opening. A visitor expecting an export guide should arrive at an export guide. Check links within the new document too; a moved page may still send people back through old addresses for its setup steps or permission reference.

Review internal links you control so they point to the final page directly where practical. Keep the redirect for people arriving through older outside links or bookmarks. Do not treat a chain of several historical moves as a good long-term navigation path. The release record should identify the final intended destination, not merely the first redirect in the chain.

Give a retired guide an honest error page

For content removed without a similar replacement, Google recommends returning 404 or 410. The fictional Route B can use a helpful error page while returning the appropriate missing-content status. The page can explain that the guide is unavailable and offer links to the current documentation. Those links help the visitor choose a next task without pretending the old answer still exists.

Do not automatically send every retired integration guide to the homepage. A homepage rarely explains the same integration question. In this example, that would make the visitor search again and could obscure the retirement decision. A clear missing-page message with useful navigation is a more honest experience when there is no relevant replacement.

Keep the page's wording bounded. If the team has verified a retirement date and migration instructions it wants to retain publicly, present them accurately on an appropriate maintained page. If those facts are not available, do not invent them to make the error look helpful. The essential statement is that the requested guide cannot be found, with a sensible route back to current information.

Repair a live document without changing its purpose

For the fictional Route C, compare a successful load with the failure state if the team can reproduce both. Does the document exist in the content system? Does the public route request the right identifier? Are the resources needed for the body available? These are proposed diagnostic questions, not a claim about the cause of an untested site's error.

Inspect the result after the repair. The body should contain the actual billing guide rather than a loading indicator, generic error or empty section. Check the relevant public path without relying on an authenticated admin view. A guide that looks complete in the editor may still fail on the public route because those are different delivery paths.

Google's HTTP status documentation says a successful response does not guarantee indexing. Treat the repaired response and restored document as evidence that the page now works. Later crawling and indexing observations are separate checks. Do not report a server fix as a proven ranking or AI citation gain.

Verify the three decisions after release

Keep one row for each route in the release record. Record the content decision, expected status, expected final address, observed status, observed final address and a short body check. In this example, the export guide should reach its new guide, the retired integration should show an honest unavailable page, and the billing guide should show its intended content.

Inspect more than the homepage and the new document list. Include the old addresses people may still follow, the current links you changed and one deliberately missing route. If the site has multiple document templates, sample each relevant template and record the limit of that sample. A check of three routes does not establish that every route on the site is correct.

Use the same record to review later Search Console feedback. An old report may reflect an earlier crawl, while a live check describes the current response. Save the dates for both. If the error persists, investigate the exact URL and rendered result reported rather than repeatedly submitting the site without checking what the crawler could receive.

Finish by giving each unresolved route an owner and a next check. A content owner may need to choose a replacement; a developer may need to repair delivery; an editor may need to remove a stale internal link. The useful result is a documentation path whose response, destination and answer agree with the reader's task. That is a concrete improvement you can verify before making any broader discovery claim.

articles.title: ModHeader in Selenium stopped working. Here's what sets HTTP headers in tests in 2026
articles.description: If your browser tests set headers through ModHeader (chrome-modheader on npm, modheader_selenium for...
articles.body_html:
If your browser tests set headers through ModHeader (chrome-modheader on npm, modheader_selenium for Python and Java), they probably broke this year, and not only because ModHeader was pulled from the stores in July. Two other things happened:

  1. The extension bundled in chrome-modheader is ModHeader 4.3.2, a Manifest V2 build. Chrome turned off MV2 extensions, so it never loads, and the package hasn't been updated since.
  2. Google Chrome 137 and newer ignore --load-extension, which is how ChromeDriver installs any extension you pass with addExtensions. Chrome for Testing and Chromium still take it.

The package still gets about 150k downloads a month, mostly from CI, so a lot of pipelines are installing something that does nothing. Here's what works now, from the simplest option up.

Request headers on every request: no extension needed

Playwright has it built in:

const context = await browser.newContext({ extraHTTPHeaders: { 'X-Env': 'staging' } });

Selenium 4 with Chrome can ask the DevTools protocol:

driver.execute_cdp_cmd('Network.enable', {})
driver.execute_cdp_cmd('Network.setExtraHTTPHeaders', {'headers': {'X-Env': 'staging'}})

Both add the headers to every request from that context or tab, which covers most "log in as a test user" and "route to staging" cases. They don't change response headers, can't remove a header the browser sends, and don't limit headers to some URLs (in Playwright, page.route() can, at the cost of handling each request in your test).

Response headers, removing headers, some URLs only

That's where an extension still earns its place: CORS or CSP response headers, stripping Referer or Cookie, a header only for api.example.com. A proxy like mitmproxy can do all of that too, but then you manage certificates, and on a cloud grid that's often not an option.

Disclosure: I maintain Headerwise, an open source (MIT) MV3 header extension, and it has an automation build for this. It has a fixed extension id, and your test sets headers by opening one URL:

chrome-extension://ogjbgamdhnjnagcdgboifgmhlgddcdce/automation.html?X-Env=staging&res:Access-Control-Allow-Origin=*

The page waits until Chrome has the rules and then reports ready. Playwright, with its own Chromium:

const ext = '/path/to/headerwise-automation';
const context = await chromium.launchPersistentContext('', {
  channel: 'chromium',
  args: [`--disable-extensions-except=${ext}`, `--load-extension=${ext}`],
});
const page = await context.newPage();
await page.goto('chrome-extension://ogjbgamdhnjnagcdgboifgmhlgddcdce/automation.html?X-Env=staging');
await page.waitForFunction(() => document.documentElement.dataset.status === 'ready');

Selenium needs Chrome for Testing, which Selenium Manager downloads when you ask for a version:

options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
options.browser_version = 'stable'
options.add_argument('--load-extension=/path/to/headerwise-automation')
driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)

If your tests are written for ModHeader

The automation build also answers ModHeader's own webdriver.modheader.com/add, /clear and /load URLs (nothing is sent to modheader.com: the browser redirects them to the extension before any request leaves) and titles the page "Done", like ModHeader did. So a test like this only changes the extension it loads:

const { getAddHeaderUrl } = require('chrome-modheader');
const options = new chrome.Options().addExtensions('headerwise-automation.crx'); // was getExtension()
options.setBrowserVersion('stable');
const driver = await new Builder().forBrowser('chrome').setChromeOptions(options).build();
await driver.get(getAddHeaderUrl('X-Env', 'staging'));
await driver.wait(until.titleIs('Done'), 10000);

The .crx is signed, so it also works on grids that take a base64 extension in the capabilities. Ask the grid for Chrome for Testing (BrowserStack calls it chromefortesting), for the same --load-extension reason.

Setup for Selenium, Playwright and Puppeteer: https://protemir.github.io/headerwise/automation.html. CI runs those snippets on every change, including one test written for ModHeader with only the extension swapped.

Which one to pick

  • Same request headers everywhere: extraHTTPHeaders or CDP. Nothing to install.
  • Response headers, removals, per-URL rules, or a lot of existing ModHeader URLs in your tests: an extension (Headerwise or whatever you trust).
  • Firefox, or traffic outside the browser too: a proxy.

If ModHeader itself got switched off in your everyday browser too, I wrote up how to get your profiles back. And if something in your test setup doesn't fit any of these, tell me in the comments.

YAYAYAYAYA!! Welcome to the 10th article of no-filter, no-sugarcoating building Crowdwide!!

  2. 38 posts
  3. 4 communities

Crowdwide is pretty much finished feature-wise, with a wide range of lists, and now only a few things are left to polish, as far as I've noticed.

So, every Sunday, a newsletter is sent to all the users who subscribed to it.

And I noticed a pattern.

The number of posts in each user's newsletter is inconsistent!

You know why??

Because I was trying to build it so that users get articles, posts, and polls in such a way that they love reading those posts and articles.

So it goes through your interests, finds what suits you best, and provides sections like:

  • Trending
  • And etc.

And it's working very well!

For those users who used Crowdwide very little or moderately, they got fewer emails. Those sections are like Trending (same for everyone) and You May Like (if you used it very little).

The mailing system is working fine as wine for now!

Also, you may have noticed that I've added some formatting options to posts!

And in emails, they appeared like this:

# Heading — listing items — ** this is bold and italic...

So I tried to remove it.

Not only from emails, but I removed it from the website too. Now you'll see the formated text or only the text, but those useless symbols won't destroy your experience.

Feeling more polished.

Isn't it? Isn't it?? Don't lie? LOL...

Also, I got some suggestions from users.

Invite your most active member to co-host one of your communities. People stick around when they have a role, not just an account.

I have never used Facebook, so idk much about it, but ngl, I feel like Facebook has a mostly older audience, and I don't think it's worth targeting them.

The second idea feels really useful because Discord and Telegram have so many channels and servers. Growing a community is really hard, so I'll try to contact some Telegram admins and Discord server owners and suggest this idea to them.

The local businesses idea also seems useful... pretty useful!!

And the fourth one...

THIS ONE IS TOO MUCH TO THE POINT!! YEAH, I BUILT CROWDWIDE FOR INDIES!! COME ON INDIESS!! IT'S YOUR CHANCE!!

All 11 users visit at intervals of 5–7 days!

2–3 users are regular daily users, mostly, from what I'm noticing in the stats!

The midnight incident 💀

I noticed that emails had stopped working!!

I didn't change anything in the code. Nothing changed in the repo.

I rechecked the whole code, like:

WHAT HAPPENED?? WHAT HAPPENED?? WHAT THE GOAT HAPPENED?? SYSTEM ROT HAPPENED?? DOT HAPPENED?? BOT HAPPENED? FORT HAPPNEDED??...

One more thing I noticed...

WOOOAHHH!!

I will not let you die, Crowdwide, that easily!
