articles.title: Passkeys are a trap? I decoded two real ones to see what a website learns
articles.description: One of the most upvoted posts on Hacker News this weekend was an essay titled "Passkeys are a trap....
articles.body_html:
One of the most upvoted posts on Hacker News this weekend was an essay titled "Passkeys are a trap. Do not use them." Its argument is not that passkeys are weak. It concedes they can be far more secure than passwords and resist man-in-the-middle attacks. The worry is control: WebAuthn lets a website ask what kind of authenticator you used, and with attestation it can demand proof, which could one day lock out custom operating systems, unofficial passkey managers or anyone a site decides not to trust.

That is a policy argument, and it is worth having. But most of the people deciding whether passkeys become a trap are not standards bodies. They are developers writing a registration endpoint. So I generated two real passkeys and decoded exactly what they tell a website.

The setup

Chromium has a virtual authenticator you can drive over the DevTools protocol, so you can create real WebAuthn credentials in a headless browser without any hardware. I registered two:

  1. A synced passkey, the kind iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager creates, with the site asking for attestation: "none".
  2. A hardware security key, with the site asking for attestation: "direct".

Then I decoded each attestationObject with this script. It needs one dependency, cbor-x.

// Decode a WebAuthn attestationObject and print what the authenticator claimed.
// Usage: node flags.mjs <base64url attestationObject>
import { decode } from "cbor-x";

const att = decode(Buffer.from(process.argv[2], "base64url"));
const auth = att.authData;           // rpIdHash(32) | flags(1) | signCount(4) | ...
const f = auth[32];

const FLAGS = [
  [0x01, "UP", "user present (someone tapped or touched)"],
  [0x04, "UV", "user verified (biometric or PIN)"],
  [0x08, "BE", "backup eligible (can be synced to other devices)"],
  [0x10, "BS", "backed up (is currently synced)"],
  [0x40, "AT", "attested credential data included"],
  [0x80, "ED", "extension data included"],
];

console.log(`attestation format: ${att.fmt}`);
console.log(`attestation statement keys: [${Object.keys(att.attStmt).join(", ")}]`);
console.log(`flags byte: 0x${f.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")}`);
for (const [bit, name, meaning] of FLAGS) {
  console.log(`  ${f & bit ? "x" : " "} ${name}  ${meaning}`);
}
console.log(`  reserved bits 0x02 and 0x20: ${f & 0x22 ? "set" : "unset"}`);

What the synced passkey said 

attestation format: none
attestation statement keys: []
flags byte: 0x5d
  x UP  user present (someone tapped or touched)
  x UV  user verified (biometric or PIN)
  x BE  backup eligible (can be synced to other devices)
  x BS  backed up (is currently synced)
  x AT  attested credential data included
    ED  extension data included

What the security key said 

attestation format: packed
attestation statement keys: [alg, sig, x5c]
flags byte: 0x45
  x UP  user present (someone tapped or touched)
  x UV  user verified (biometric or PIN)
    BE  backup eligible (can be synced to other devices)
    BS  backed up (is currently synced)
  x AT  attested credential data included
    ED  extension data included

Three things stand out.

The flags are self-reported. With fmt: none the statement is empty. Nothing signs the claim that the user was verified or that the key is synced. The site simply takes the authenticator's word for it. That is the article's point: without attestation, software can say anything, and a site that wants certainty has to ask for attestation.

AT does not mean attested. This trips people up. The AT bit means the authenticator data contains the new credential's ID and public key. It is set on every registration, including the one with no attestation at all.

Attestation is a certificate chain. The security key returned x5c, an X.509 chain that identifies the authenticator's maker and, through its AAGUID, its model. A site can check it against the FIDO Metadata Service and refuse anything it does not recognise. That is the lever the article worries about.

Who actually pulls the lever

You do, in one line. Here is the default in SimpleWebAuthn, a widely used WebAuthn server library for Node:

import { generateRegistrationOptions } from "@simplewebauthn/server";

const options = await generateRegistrationOptions({
  rpName: "Acme",
  rpID: "acme.com",
  userName: user.email,
  attestationType: "none", // the default in v14; "direct" asks for the certificate chain
  authenticatorSelection: {
    residentKey: "preferred",
    userVerification: "preferred",
  },
});

The WebAuthn standard's own default for attestation conveyance is also none. Level 3 of the spec, which added the backup flags, became a W3C Recommendation on 25 August 2026. And even if you ask for attestation, Apple's synced passkeys do not provide it, according to passkey vendor Corbado. A consumer site that required attestation would lock out a large share of iPhone users on day one. So for consumer products today, the trap is mostly theoretical. Enterprises are the exception: requiring attested hardware keys for employees is a legitimate, common policy.

The rules I use for client apps

  1. Leave attestation at none for consumers. Only ask for it when a contract or regulator requires specific hardware.
  2. Never make passkeys the only way in. Keep a recovery path: a second passkey, TOTP or a verified email link. The article recommends TOTP and hardware keys, and supporting them costs you little.
  3. Accept any authenticator. Do not allowlist by AAGUID unless you have a reason you can write down. An allowlist quietly breaks every passkey manager you did not think of, and the user only finds out at the login screen. Bitwarden, 1Password, KeePassXC and the platform managers should all work.
  4. Read BE and BS, do not enforce them. They are useful for UX. If a user's only passkey has BS unset, it lives on one device, and losing that device means losing the account. Prompt them to add a backup or a second factor. Do not reject the credential.

Passkeys are the biggest phishing fix in a decade, and most of the control the article fears sits in the options object you write. Write it so your users can leave.

I set up authentication like this in every MVP we build at Axionry, and the rest of my default stack is in the SaaS MVP tech stack for 2026.

Sources: Passkeys are a trap (Non-Functional, 10 October 2026), Hacker News discussion, W3C Web Authentication Level 3, SimpleWebAuthn, Corbado on platforms without passkey attestation. Registrations generated with Chromium's virtual authenticator on 12 October 2026. I used an AI assistant while drafting this.

articles.title: string.length is wrong for X and Bluesky. My counter failed 8 of 34 tests against X's own library
articles.description: I'm Alex. I build Fuxux, a social media scheduler: you write a post once and it goes out to X,...
articles.body_html:
I'm Alex. I build Fuxux, a social media scheduler: you write a post once and it goes out to X, Bluesky, Instagram, LinkedIn, Threads and a few more.

A scheduler has to answer one boring question before anything is sent: does this text fit? I assumed that was text.length <= limit. It isn't, and the two networks with the smallest limits are the two where it goes wrong.

I also thought I had already solved it. Then I sat down to write this post, checked my own code against X's library to get the examples right, and it was wrong on 8 of 34 strings. So this is the corrected version, with the mistake left in.

Three ways to count one string

Take ok 👍🏽. That's "ok", a space, and a thumbs up with a skin tone.

const text = "ok 👍🏽";

text.length;        // 7  UTF-16 code units
[...text].length;   // 5  code points
[...new Intl.Segmenter(undefined, { granularity: "grapheme" })
  .segment(text)].length; // 4  what a person sees

Three honest answers. Which one a network uses decides whether your post is accepted.

String length X counts Bluesky counts
ok 👍🏽 7 5 4
👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 (family) 11 2 1
🇪🇸 (flag) 4 2 1
こんにちは 5 10 5
𝗯𝗼𝗹𝗱 (bold "font") 8 8 4
read fuxux.com now 18 32 18
a 140-character URL 140 23 140

The X column is from X's own library. The Bluesky column is the grapheme count.

X: weights, not characters

X publishes how it counts in an open source library, twitter-text. The limit is 280, but 280 of a weighted unit:

  • Latin letters, digits and common punctuation weigh 1. In code point terms: U+0000 to U+10FF, U+2000 to U+200D, U+2010 to U+201F and U+2032 to U+2037.
  • Everything else weighs 2. That's why five Japanese characters cost 10, and why those bold "fonts" people paste into bios cost double: they are mathematical letters far outside the Latin range.
  • An emoji weighs 2, as a whole. A family of four is seven code points glued with joiners and it is still 2.
  • Any link weighs 23, whether it is 9 characters or 140.
  • The text is normalised to NFC first, so e plus a combining accent counts as one é.

The link rule bites in two directions. A long URL is cheaper than it looks. A short one is more expensive: fuxux.com is 9 characters and costs 23.

And it catches text you didn't mean as a link. It works.So does this is 21 characters. X counts 36, because a missing space after the full stop makes works.So look like a domain (.so is a real ending).

Where I got it wrong

My first version walked the string one code point at a time and added 1 or 2:

function weigh(text) {
  let total = 0;
  for (const char of text) total += xWeight(char.codePointAt(0));
  return total;
}

That handles a plain 👍 (one code point, weight 2). It falls apart on anything built from several:

String X My first version
ok 👍🏽 5 7
👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 2 11
🇪🇸 2 4
1️⃣ 2 5
❤️ 2 4

It always over-counted, so nobody could post something too long because of it. It just told people their post didn't fit when it did. On a 280 limit, a few emoji with skin tones is enough to matter.

The fix is to split into graphemes first, and count a grapheme that is an emoji as 2 no matter what it is made of:

const segmenter = new Intl.Segmenter(undefined, { granularity: "grapheme" });

// Drawn as an emoji by default, or a symbol followed by the emoji
// selector, or a flag letter, or a keycap like 1️⃣.
const EMOJI =
  /\p{Emoji_Presentation}|\p{Extended_Pictographic}️|\p{Regional_Indicator}|[0-9#*]️?⃣/u;

function xWeight(cp) {
  return (cp <= 0x10ff) ||
    (cp >= 0x2000 && cp <= 0x200d) ||
    (cp >= 0x2010 && cp <= 0x201f) ||
    (cp >= 0x2032 && cp <= 0x2037) ? 1 : 2;
}

function weigh(text) {
  let total = 0;
  for (const { segment } of segmenter.segment(text)) {
    if (EMOJI.test(segment)) { total += 2; continue; }
    for (const char of segment) total += xWeight(char.codePointAt(0));
  }
  return total;
}

function countForX(text, urlPattern) {
  const s = text.normalize("NFC");
  let total = 0, last = 0;
  for (const m of s.matchAll(urlPattern)) {
    total += weigh(s.slice(last, m.index)) + 23;
    last = m.index + m[0].length;
  }
  return total + weigh(s.slice(last));
}

My second attempt was also wrong, in a smaller way. I used \p{Extended_Pictographic} on its own, and © 2026 came out as 7 instead of 6. A bare © is in that Unicode class, but X only treats it as an emoji when the emoji selector (U+FE0F) follows it. Same for a text heart ❤ versus ❤️. Hence the longer pattern above.

It now matches twitter-text on 43 of my 44 test strings. The one it misses is a link ending I don't carry: X knows every domain ending there is, and I keep a short list of the common ones, so a.community is a link to X and plain text to me. If you need that last case, use their list.

Which is the real advice here: if you can ship the dependency, call twitter.parseTweet(text).weightedLength and be done. I wanted something small that runs in the browser as you type, so I wrote my own and test it against theirs.

Bluesky: graphemes, and a second limit behind it

Bluesky's limit is 300, and it counts graphemes. The post schema says so directly: maxGraphemes: 300. So the family emoji is 1, the flag is 1, and ok 👍🏽 is 4. Intl.Segmenter gives you that number in every current browser and in Node.

The same schema also has maxLength: 3000, and that one is in UTF-8 bytes. Normal text never gets near it. Three hundred family emoji would, at 25 bytes each.

The rest

For Instagram, LinkedIn, Threads, Facebook and the others I count text.length. I have not checked each of them emoji by emoji the way I just did for X, so I won't claim more than that. Their limits are large enough (500 on Threads, 2,200 on Instagram, 3,000 on LinkedIn) that a few units either way rarely decides anything. On 280 and 300 it does.

Try it

The counter is free and needs no account: fuxux.com/tools/character-counter. Paste a post and it shows the count for each network side by side, using the rules above. Paste ok 👍🏽 and you'll see X and Bluesky disagree.

The limits in it are the same numbers Fuxux uses when it publishes. If you'd rather not think about any of this, that's what the scheduler is for, and there's a free plan (3 social accounts, 5 posts a month, no card).

If you know a string where X's count surprised you, put it in the comments. I'll add it to the tests.

articles.title: Your Nuxt layers are leaking, and your linter can't see it
articles.description: Here is a Vue component. Spot the architecture bug.    <!--...
articles.body_html:
Here is a Vue component. Spot the architecture bug.

<!-- lyears/admin/app/components/AdminPanel.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
  const cart = useCart();
</script>

<template>
  <CartSummary />
</template>

Looks fine, right? No weird imports. Nothing red in the editor. ESLint is happy. The PR gets approved.

The problem: useCart and <CartSummary> live in the shop layer. The admin layer was never supposed to touch shop. You just tied two parts of your app together, and nobody noticed. Not you, not the reviewer, not a single tool in the pipeline.

Do that thirty more times and your nice modular Nuxt app is one big ball of yarn with a layers/ folder on top.

Why nothing catches it

Nuxt layers are a great way to split a big app: a shared layer for the design system, an auth layer, a shop layer, an admin layer. You get a modular monolith for free.

But the modular part only holds if each layer stays in its lane. And the tools that guard boundaries (ESLint import rules, dependency-cruiser and friends) all read import statements.

In Nuxt, most dependencies have no import statement. Composables, utils, components and Nitro server utils are auto-imported. The boundary tool looks at the file, sees zero imports, and gives it a gold star.

I hit this on a real project. After a few months, "admin may only use shared and auth" was a rule that lived in a README and nowhere else.

So I built layerscope

layerscope resolves auto-imports the same way Nuxt does, and fails CI when a layer uses something it is not allowed to.

You write the rules once:

// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  modules: ['nuxt-layerscope'],
  layerscope: {
    layers: {
      shared: { allow: [] },
      auth: { allow: ['shared'] },
      shop: { allow: ['shared', 'auth'] },
      admin: { allow: ['shared', 'auth'] },
    },
  },
});

Then run:

npx layerscope check --prepare

And the component from the top of this post finally gets caught:

layers/admin/app/components/AdminPanel.vue
  2:14    error  Auto-import "useCart" crosses from layer "admin" into "shop"  layer-boundary
                 useCart → layers/shop/app/composables/useCart.ts
                 allowed for "admin": shared, auth
  8:5     error  Component <CartSummary> crosses from layer "admin" into "shop"  layer-boundary
                 CartSummary → layers/shop/app/components/CartSummary.vue
                 allowed for "admin": shared, auth

It tells you what crossed, where it came from, and what the layer is allowed to use. No guessing.

How it knows

layerscope does not guess from file names. A small Nuxt module records what Nuxt actually registered: every component, every auto-import, every server util, per layer. So layer priority, overridden components, pathPrefix, custom component dirs and module auto-imports like @vueuse/nuxt all come out the way Nuxt sees them.

Then it parses your scripts with oxc and your templates with the real Vue compiler, tracks scope (a local const useCart shadows the auto-import, same as at runtime), and checks every edge against your rules.

If it can't resolve something, it says so. It never quietly calls an unknown reference "safe".

On a test project with 3,000 source files in 10 layers, a full check takes about 770 ms.

"But my project already has 200 violations"

Same. That is why there is a baseline.

npx layerscope init --baseline

init looks at your layers, writes a config that allows exactly what exists today, and accepts the current findings. Your first CI run is green. From now on, only new violations fail the build. Delete a line from the config when you want to fix that dependency for real.

The GitHub Action even adds a summary like adds 3, fixes 5 and Baseline: 47 → 42, so you can watch the mess shrink one PR at a time.

The fun extras

  • layerscope why useCart shows every place a symbol is used, and which uses break the rules. Great before you move a composable.
  • layerscope graph draws the dependency graph between your layers.
  • layerscope unused finds things nothing depends on.
  • A Nuxt DevTools tab with findings, the layer graph and symbol traces. It updates when you save. Try the live demo.
  • Cycle detection, presets, an ESLint plugin, SARIF output for the GitHub Security tab, and an MCP server so your coding assistant can ask "may I use this here?" before it writes the code.

Works with Nuxt 3 and 4, and with local, npm and git layers.

Try it in five minutes 

npx nuxi module add nuxt-layerscope --dev
npx layerscope init --baseline
npx layerscope check --prepare

Or poke at the example project on StackBlitz first. It has four layers and one violation for each rule.

  • Docs: https://layerscope.kitdev.space/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/hamedniroomand/nuxt-layerscope
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/nuxt-layerscope

It is MIT and still young (0.x), so bug reports and weird edge cases are very welcome. If your layers have a secret you want to find out, run it and tell me how many violations you got. I promise not to judge. Much.

articles.title: I Bridged My Real Logged-In Browser to Chrome's New WebMCP API
articles.description: I Bridged My Real Logged-In Browser to Chrome's New WebMCP API   Chrome's WebMCP proposal...
articles.body_html:
I Bridged My Real Logged-In Browser to Chrome's New WebMCP API

Chrome's WebMCP proposal (W3C Community Group draft, origin trial from M149) lets a web page declare typed, callable tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() — so an in-browser AI agent can call them directly instead of scraping the DOM. The official demo shows toy tools like a "greet" function. Fun, but not something you can ship.

I wanted the real thing: my actual browser, with my real sessions and cookies, exposed as WebMCP tools. So I built webmcp-bridge — the first bridge from Browser Buddy (my tool that reads your logged-in Chrome through a native host, listed on awesome-mcp-servers) to the WebMCP API.

How it works

A tiny localhost server (stdlib-only Python, no dependencies) maps Browser Buddy's tools to WebMCP-style endpoints:

  • GET /webmcp/tools → tool manifests (name, title, description, inputSchema, annotations)
  • POST /webmcp/tools/call → forwards to the Browser Buddy native host over its Unix socket

A page-side JS shim (webmcp.js) fetches the manifests and registers each tool with document.modelContext.registerTool() (falling back to navigator.modelContext on Chrome 146-era preview builds). From there, any WebMCP-capable agent discovers and calls them like any other page tool.

Two tools ship out of the box:

  • read_active_tab — read the user's active Chrome tab (URL, title, cleaned text).
  • open_and_read_url — open a URL in a background tab with the real profile (cookies/sessions included), extract readable text, close the tab. Pages behind logins, paywalls-with-session, and bot checks become callable tools.

Why not just scrape?

Because login walls, 403s, and bot detection defeat server-side fetchers — and DOM scraping is fragile by design. The tools run in your browser as you, so what you can see, the agent can read.

Security, since this opens your real browser

  • The server binds 127.0.0.1 only; the shim is same-origin by design.
  • open_and_read_url enforces a domain allowlist (~/.config/webmcp-bridge/config.json, allowed_domains). Empty means everything is allowed — with a warning baked into the tool result so an agent can see it's wide open.

Try it 

pip install webmcp-bridge
webmcp-bridge   # http://127.0.0.1:18765/ — demo page included

Then on any page:

<script src="http://127.0.0.1:18765/webmcp.js"></script>

15 smoke tests, all green. MIT licensed. Stdlib-only Python (the JS shim is allowed to exist — WebMCP is a browser-side API).

Repo: https://github.com/hahahahahahahahah6/webmcp-bridge
PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/webmcp-bridge/

articles.title: Security Regression Gate Sentinel — block the rise, not the presence
articles.description: Security Regression Gate — block the rise, not the presence   How Sentinel decides which...
articles.body_html:
Security Regression Gate — block the rise, not the presence

How Sentinel decides which merge requests get stopped in CI: not "this file can run shell commands" (that's been true for months), but "this change just gave the file a power it did not have yesterday".

Where the numbers come from. Everything here was measured on 2026-10-12, on the master branch of the Sentinel repository, using Node 24.19.0. I used three sources and I name the source at each number:

  1. Unit tests, run for real with node --test. I did not count test( lines with grep.
  2. A replay of today's gate over all 118 merge requests ever merged into Sentinel's master. This is deterministic, offline and takes one command (see Captured output).
  3. An earlier evaluation on 16 public GitHub repositories and 5 GitLab ones, written up in the repo's design-partner notes. That one was produced by a throwaway script that lives outside the repo, so nobody has reproduced it independently yet. I say this again wherever I use those numbers.

There are no CI pipeline statistics in this article (how often the job actually failed on real MRs). I didn't have read access to the pipeline API while writing, so the article doesn't claim any.

Part 1 — For humans

The smoke detector that screams at candles

Imagine a smoke detector that goes off every time it sees a candle. Not smoke. Not fire. A candle that's been on the same table for three years.

The first day, you jump. The second day, you sigh. By the end of the week you've taken the battery out, and now you have no smoke detector at all.

Most "security scanners" in code review work this way. They read a file, see something dangerous-sounding ("this file can run other programs!"), and raise a flag. They raise it again the next time someone fixes a typo in that file, and the time after that. The file was always able to run other programs. The flag carries no new information, so people learn to ignore it. Once a team ignores the warnings, the scanner has stopped doing anything useful.

Sentinel's merge-request gate is built around the opposite question. It doesn't ask "is this file dangerous?" It asks:

"Did this change make the file more dangerous than it was before?"

That's the whole idea of this article. The rest is detail: how "more dangerous" is measured, what happens when the answer is yes, and the cases where the gate still doesn't see the problem. I list those too.

What Sentinel is, in one paragraph

Sentinel is an autonomous agent that watches a JavaScript codebase (its own, mostly) and decides, file by file, whether to leave it alone or propose a change. An earlier article in this series covered how it avoids re-thinking the same thought (the Novelty Gate). This one leaves the agent's head and goes to the front door of the codebase: the merge request. That's the moment a human (or an agent) asks "please add my change to the main branch". The gate lives in CI, the automated checklist that runs on every merge request. If the gate says no, the merge button stays grey.

The gate uses no AI. No language model is asked whether the code "looks risky". It's a plain program that reads code structure, and it gives the same answer every time you run it on the same input. That matters for a reason I'll come back to: you can argue with a deterministic gate, and you can reproduce its behaviour. You can't reproduce a mood.

A ladder with four rungs

To say "more dangerous", you need a scale. Sentinel uses four levels, decided purely by what the code can do:

level in plain words examples
low only computes, or only reads math, formatting, reading a config file
medium changes something outside itself writing files, talking to the network, handling passwords or crypto
high can destroy things deleting files
critical can do anything running other programs, or running text as code

That last row is the interesting one. A file that can start another program (a shell command, git, ffmpeg) or turn a string into running code (eval) has no meaningful upper limit on what it can do. So the ladder stops there. You can't be "more critical than critical".

Each changed file gets two readings: one before the merge request, one after. The gate compares the two.

The rule, in plain words

A merge request gets blocked when one of its files ends up at critical and at least one of these is true:

  1. It climbed. It was low, medium or high before, and now it's critical. "This file couldn't run programs yesterday. Today it can."
  2. It was already critical and gained a new kind of power. Say it could already run programs, and now it can also turn text into code. Same rung on the ladder, new trick. "This file could already run programs. Now it can also execute arbitrary strings."

A merge request does not get blocked when:

  • a critical file is edited without gaining any new dangerous power (fixing a typo, renaming a variable, adding a log line),
  • a dangerous power is removed (going down the ladder is always fine),
  • a file moves up the ladder but stays below critical. This one is a deliberate choice, explained under The honest part.

Put another way, the gate reacts to the candle being lit. It doesn't react to a candle that has been sitting on the table for three years.

The permission slip

Some files should run programs. Sentinel's own report script has to ask git for the old and new version of each file, and there's no way to do that without running git. Blocking that file forever would be silly.

For these files the repository keeps a small permission-slip file called .sentinel-gate.json. Each entry says which file, why, and exactly which powers are accepted:

{
  "acknowledged": {
    "scripts/mr-report.js": {
      "reason": "Reads git objects through execFileSync('git', ...) — the report has no other way to see both revisions of a file, and the arguments are never user input.",
      "facts": ["child_process", "process_spawn"]
    }
  }
}

That's the real file from the repository (one of its two entries). It says: this file may import the process-spawning module and may spawn processes. It does not say "this file may do anything". If someone later adds eval to that file, the slip doesn't cover it and the gate blocks again.

The slip also sits in the repository, next to the code. Someone has to write the reason down, a reviewer can read it, and the version history shows who added it and when.

The honest part: what the gate does not see

A gate is only as useful as its known weaknesses are known. These are written down in the repo, and each one is pinned by a test that passes (more on that in Part 3):

1. Climbing slowly below the top rung. If one merge request takes a file from low to medium (it starts writing files), and the next takes it from medium to high (it starts deleting files), a gate set to "critical" says nothing. Neither step reached the top. The report still shows both climbs, and the team can set the gate stricter (high instead of critical) to catch exactly this. It's a dial, not a hidden bug. The CI job in Sentinel's own repo is set to critical, so in that repo deleting files is reported but not blocked.

2. Two files working together. The gate reads each file on its own. If file A gets a function that runs a program (blocked, or explicitly allowed once), and a later merge request makes file B call that function, file B looks harmless. File B didn't change its own powers, it just borrowed A's. Seeing that needs a map of who calls whom across the whole codebase. That's a different, bigger tool, and the project's own planning document explicitly lists it under "what not to build yet".

3. The old-style permission slip. Older slips just say "this file is fine, here's why", without a list of powers. They still work, so old setups don't suddenly break. The catch is that a new power on such a file is accepted too. The gate now prints that acceptance in the merge request comment, along with the power it absorbed, so nobody can say they weren't told. Sentinel's own slips use the precise form.

4. Code the parser can't read. If a file uses syntax the JavaScript parser doesn't understand (TypeScript-style type annotations in a .js file, for example), the report says "not analysed" for that file. It doesn't guess. The flip side is that an unreadable file is never blocked. I checked while writing this: a file that gains both child_process and a type annotation comes out as parsed: false and doesn't trip the gate. It is clearly marked in the report, but it isn't stopped.

There used to be two more items on this list. An audit in September found that (a) adding a second dangerous power to an already-critical file slipped through, because "critical → critical" counted as "unchanged". It also found that (b) a permission slip for "runs programs" quietly covered a later eval too. Both were turned into passing tests that documented the hole, and then both were fixed in a follow-up merge request. That's the rule from point 2 above ("already critical and gained a new kind of power") and the precise permission slip. That order — first prove the hole with a test, then close it — is how this project likes to work.

Does it actually catch anything?

Three different measurements, in increasing order of "you can check this yourself":

Other people's code (not independently reproduced yet). The detector was run over the last 15 merged pull requests of 16 well-known public JavaScript projects (express, fastify, axios, Ghost, strapi, and others). That's 140 pull requests with JavaScript changes. On the first run, it would have blocked 10 of them, and when someone read all 10 by hand, only 3 were real. The other 7 were false alarms. Precision: 30%. That was embarrassing, and it was useful. Every one of the false alarms had the same cause, which I'll explain in Part 2. After fixing that cause, the same 140 pull requests produced 3 blocks (2%), all 3 genuine, and every changed file that really runs commands was flagged: 28 of 28. On five GitLab-hosted projects it blocked 5 merge requests, all 5 genuine when read by hand.

Sentinel's own history (reproducible with one command). I replayed today's gate over all 118 merge requests ever merged into Sentinel's master. 93 of them changed JavaScript. The gate would have blocked 3. All three are real "this file can now run programs" moments: a capture tool that shells out to an external binary, a benchmark sample that spawns workers, and a test helper that runs a child process. Two more raises were waived by the permission slip (the report script itself and a CLI test). Not one of the 118 merge requests had the "already critical, gained a new power" pattern, so the fix from the audit has never fired on real history. It's pinned by tests, not by luck.

Live production. The gate runs in CI, not inside the running agent, so the production dashboard doesn't count gate blocks at all. I won't invent a number for it.

The other gate with the same name

The name of this article is a little unfair to a module that already exists. In Sentinel's source code, the class actually called SecurityRegressionGate isn't the CI gate. It's a sibling that lives inside the agent. When Sentinel proposes a change to its own code (say, "make this login check faster"), that sibling compares the old and new version and refuses the change if a security safeguard got weaker. Examples: a constant-time comparison disappeared, there are fewer input checks than before, or a "remember the answer" shortcut now skips the real password check.

It's the same philosophy from the other side. The CI gate blocks when danger goes up. The runtime gate blocks when protection goes down. Neither one cares that danger or protection exists. Both compare a before with an after. I cover it briefly in Part 2, because it shares the idea but not the code.

The 30-second version

  • The gate compares each changed file before vs after the merge request.
  • It blocks when a file reaches critical (can run programs or execute text as code), or gains a new dangerous power while already critical.
  • Editing a dangerous file without making it more dangerous is free. Removing danger is always free.
  • Intended risk is accepted per file and per power, with a written reason, in the repo.
  • Known blind spots, all written down and tested: slow climbing below the threshold, two files cooperating, old-style slips, and files the parser can't read.
  • No AI is involved and the result is deterministic: on Sentinel's own 118 merge requests it would have blocked 3, all genuine.

Two properties are worth stating before the code:

  • The pure layer (libs/mr-report/index.js) does no I/O. No network, no LLM, no filesystem, no git. The caller hands it both revisions of every file as strings. There's a test that enforces this (Part 3).

Step 1 — what changed, against what 

// scripts/mr-report.js:78-88
function changedJsFiles(baseRev, headRev) {
    const mergeBase = git(["merge-base", baseRev, headRev]).trim();
    const names = git(["diff", "--name-only", "--diff-filter=ACMRD", mergeBase, headRev])
        .split("\n")
        .map(name => name.trim())
        .filter(Boolean)
        .filter(name => name.endsWith(".js"))
        .filter(name => !name.startsWith("node_modules/"));

    return { mergeBase, files: names.map(file => ({ path: file, before: blob(mergeBase, file), after: blob(headRev, file) })) };
}

Three details are doing real work here:

  • git merge-base, not the target branch tip. If master moved on after the branch was cut, diffing against the tip would credit (or blame) the merge request for other people's commits. The merge base is "what this branch actually started from".
  • --diff-filter=ACMRD means Added, Copied, Modified, Renamed, Deleted. Deleted files go through the diff too, so removing a dangerous file shows up as a lowered risk instead of vanishing silently.
  • A missing revision is the empty string: 
// scripts/mr-report.js:70-76
function blob(rev, file) {
    try {
        return git(["show", `${rev}:${file}`], "ignore");
    } catch {
        return "";
    }
}

An empty source parses to empty facts, so an added file is simply "low → whatever it is now". That's the right baseline: a brand-new file that spawns processes did raise the risk of the repository.

Only .js is in scope. .ts, .mjs and .cjs aren't analysed today, and that's a deliberate, stated scope, not an oversight.

Step 2 — facts from syntax, not from substrings

Each revision goes through AstFacts.extract, a tree-sitter walk that records operations (booleans like processSpawn, dynamicEval, diskDelete) and derives two things from them:

// libs/core/ast-facts.js:553-561
function dangerousOf(operations) {
    const dangerous = [];
    if (operations.dynamicEval) dangerous.push("eval");
    if (operations.childProcess) dangerous.push("child_process");
    if (operations.processSpawn) dangerous.push("process_spawn");
    if (operations.processExit) dangerous.push("process.exit");
    if (operations.diskDelete) dangerous.push("destructive_fs");
    return dangerous;
}

// libs/core/ast-facts.js:570-579
function riskOf(facts) {
    const operations = facts?.operations || {};

    if (operations.dynamicEval || operations.processSpawn || operations.childProcess) return "critical";
    if (operations.diskDelete) return "high";
    if (operations.diskWrite) return "medium";
    if (operations.outboundHttp || operations.inboundHttp) return "medium";
    if (operations.cryptoUse || operations.secretComparison) return "medium";
    return "low";
}

dangerous is the list of fact families: eval, child_process, process_spawn, process.exit, destructive_fs. Acknowledgements use exactly these names, and they're what the gate compares when a file is already critical.

Note the third condition in the critical line: childProcess. It's set by the import alone, before anything is called:

// libs/core/ast-facts.js:348-362 (visitCall)
    // require("child_process") / import("fs") / require("fs") -> imports
    const importer = !object && (property === "require" || property === "import");
    if (importer) {
        const source = stringLiteral(callArgs[0]);
        if (source) {
            imports.add(source);
            if (CHILD_PROCESS_MODULES.has(source)) {
                const evidence = `${property}(child_process)`;
                facts.operations.childProcess = true;
                calls.process.add(evidence);
                signal("child_process_import", evidence, node);
            }
        }
        return;
    }

with CHILD_PROCESS_MODULES = new Set(["child_process", "node:child_process"]). A bare const { exec } = require("child_process") is critical by itself. This is what makes the "import in one MR, call in the next" trick fail on the first MR (scenario 1a in the tests).

The bug that made precision 30%

The first version decided processSpawn by the callee's name. exec, spawn, fork → spawning. Then it met real code:

  • schemaAndHostRegExp.exec(url): RegExp.prototype.exec, probably one of the most-called methods in JavaScript,
  • cluster.fork(),
  • a locally defined function exec(script, stds) in pm2 that only wires up logging,
  • bundled editor code full of regex .exec.

Seven out of ten blocks on public repositories were regular expressions and local helpers. If you've ever been paged because a regex was "executing", you know the feeling.

The fix was binding resolution: a call is process spawning when it's bound to a spawning module, not when it happens to share a name with one.

// libs/core/ast-facts.js:48-60
const SPAWN_FUNCTIONS = new Set([
    "exec", "execSync", "execFile", "execFileSync", "spawn", "spawnSync", "fork", "execFileAsync"
]);

// `regex.exec(input)` and `cluster.fork()` share their names with the
// child_process API, so these two are only process spawning when the callee is
// bound to a spawning module. The rest of SPAWN_FUNCTIONS is unambiguous enough
// to flag on the bare name.
const SPAWN_ONLY_WHEN_BOUND = new Set(["exec", "fork"]);

const SPAWN_MODULES = new Set([
    "child_process", "node:child_process", "cross-spawn", "execa", "shelljs", "zx"
]);

// libs/core/ast-facts.js:326-341
function isSpawnCall({ object, property, raw }, host, spawnBindings) {
    if (!property) return false;

    // Anything imported from a spawning module spawns, whatever it is called.
    if (object ? spawnBindings.modules.has(host) : spawnBindings.functions.has(property)) return true;

    if (!SPAWN_FUNCTIONS.has(property)) return false;

    if (object) {
        // require("child_process").exec(...), childProcess.spawn(...)
        if (/child_process/.test(raw)) return true;
        return !SPAWN_ONLY_WHEN_BOUND.has(property) && /^(child_?process|cp)$/i.test(host);
    }

    return !SPAWN_ONLY_WHEN_BOUND.has(property);
}

spawnBindings is collected in a pre-pass over require / destructuring (including renames like const { exec: run } = require("child_process")) / import statements. After the fix the same 140 public PRs blocked 3 instead of 10, and the "really executes commands" recall check (a file whose text both imports a spawning module and calls one of its functions) stayed at 28/28. Again: those numbers come from the design-partner write-up, produced by a script outside the repo, and haven't been reproduced independently.

Step 3 — diff the facts, then the risk 

// libs/mr-report/index.js:62-69
function riskDelta(before, after) {
    const direction = RISK_ORDER.indexOf(after) - RISK_ORDER.indexOf(before);
    return {
        before,
        after,
        direction: direction > 0 ? "raised" : direction < 0 ? "lowered" : "unchanged"
    };
}

with RISK_ORDER = ["low", "medium", "high", "critical"]. Every fact family is diffed as a set (added = after \ before, removed = before \ after), never as a text diff. That's why a formatting-only change reports nothing: same sets on both sides, factCount: 0.

// libs/mr-report/index.js:76-91 (abridged)
function diffFacts({ path, before = "", after = "" }) {
    const factsBefore = AstFacts.extract(before);
    const factsAfter = AstFacts.extract(after);
    const parsed = Boolean(factsBefore.ast && factsAfter.ast);

    const finding = {
        path,
        parsed,
        // routes, env, exports, imports: { added, removed } ...
        dangerous: { added: added(factsBefore.dangerous, factsAfter.dangerous), removed: added(factsAfter.dangerous, factsBefore.dangerous) },
        operations: operationDelta(factsBefore.operations, factsAfter.operations),
        risk: riskDelta(AstFacts.riskOf(factsBefore), AstFacts.riskOf(factsAfter))
    };
    // ...
}

Notice that risk alone saturates: once a file is critical, direction can only be unchanged or lowered. That's exactly why the September audit found a hole, and why dangerous.added had to join the trigger.

Step 4 — the decision 

// libs/mr-report/index.js:144-150
function gated(result, threshold) {
    return result.findings.filter(f =>
        f.parsed
        && RISK_ORDER.indexOf(f.risk.after) >= threshold
        && (f.risk.direction === "raised" || f.dangerous.added.length > 0)
    );
}

Read it as a truth table, at --gate critical:

before → after dangerous.added candidate? why
low → critical child_process yes raised to the threshold
critical → critical [] no level alone never triggers
critical → critical process_spawn yes new family at the threshold
critical → low [] no lowered
medium → high destructive_fs no below the threshold (--gate high: yes)
anything, parsed: false — no not analysed, not guessed

Then acknowledgements:

// libs/mr-report/index.js:152-182
function acknowledgement(entry) {
    if (typeof entry === "string") return { reason: entry, facts: null };
    if (entry && typeof entry === "object" && typeof entry.reason === "string") {
        return { reason: entry.reason, facts: Array.isArray(entry.facts) ? entry.facts : null };
    }
    return null;
}

function covers(ack, finding) {
    if (!ack) return false;
    if (ack.facts === null) return true;
    return finding.dangerous.added.every(fact => ack.facts.includes(fact));
}

function gate(result, level = "critical", acknowledged = {}) {
    const threshold = RISK_ORDER.indexOf(level);
    const candidates = gated(result, threshold);
    const offenders = [];
    const waived = [];

    for (const f of candidates) {
        const ack = acknowledgement(acknowledged[f.path]);
        if (covers(ack, f)) {
            waived.push({ path: f.path, risk: f.risk, reason: ack.reason, facts: f.dangerous.added });
        } else {
            offenders.push(f);
        }
    }

    return { level, offenders, waived, blocked: offenders.length > 0 };
}

Things worth noticing:

  • covers is every, not some. An ack for child_process doesn't cover a finding that adds child_process and eval.
  • facts: null means legacy. A bare string waives the whole path. That's the "old-style permission slip" from Part 1. It isn't silent: waived[] carries the absorbed facts, and renderGate prints every waiver.
  • A malformed .sentinel-gate.json means nothing is acknowledged, not everything: 
// scripts/mr-report.js:49-57
function acknowledgedRisks() {
    try {
        const raw = fs.readFileSync(path.join(REPO_ROOT, ".sentinel-gate.json"), "utf8");
        const parsed = JSON.parse(raw).acknowledged;
        return parsed && typeof parsed === "object" ? parsed : {};
    } catch {
        return {};
    }
}

A typo in the permission file fails closed: you get blocked, not waved through. That's the right direction for a security gate, and the annoying direction for whoever made the typo.

  • The ack is read from the checkout under analysis, so it's the merge request's own version of .sentinel-gate.json that counts. Adding an entry to that file is part of the diff and shows up in review. It's not a hidden config somewhere else. (It also means a merge request can acknowledge its own risk. The defence against that is a human reading the JSON in the diff. The gate makes the decision visible, but it doesn't take it away from people.)

The runtime sibling: SecurityRegressionGate

Inside the agent, on the EVOLVE path (after the syntactic ShadowGuard, before simulation and governance), a separate module asks the inverse question: did this patch weaken a protection that was there before?

// libs/core/security-regression-gate.js:73-100 (abridged)
evaluate({ oldCode = "", newCode = "", envelope = {} } = {}) {
    if (!newCode) return { regression: false, reason: "no-new-code" };
    if (!oldCode) return { regression: false, reason: "no-baseline" };

    const keepSecurity = isSecuritySensitive(envelope);

    // 1. A security primitive present in the baseline is dropped/reduced.
    for (const primitive of SECURITY_PRIMITIVES) {
        const before = countOccurrences(oldCode, primitive);
        const after = countOccurrences(newCode, primitive);
        if (before > after) {
            const tag = primitive.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9]/g, "");
            return { regression: true, reason: `security_regression:weakened-${tag}`, keepSecurity };
        }
    }

    // 2. Input validation / error handling removed.
    if (countThrows(oldCode) > countThrows(newCode)) {
        return { regression: true, reason: "security_regression:removed-validation", keepSecurity };
    }
    // 3. (keep_security targets only) a new `cache[...]` + `return true` shortcut -> verification-bypass
    // ...
}

SECURITY_PRIMITIVES is a list of names like timingSafeEqual, pbkdf2, scrypt, randomBytes, createHmac, bcrypt, argon2, sanitize, escapeHtml, csrf, helmet. The executor turns a regression into a hard local REJECT, records a SECURITY_REGRESSION trauma and rollback, and attributes the rejection to "security-regression-gate" in analytics.

Same shape as the CI gate: before vs after, react to the delta. Different instrument: this one uses substring and throw counts, not an AST. It's coarse on purpose, and it fails in the safe direction. A false REJECT only postpones an auto-evolution, and the module's own header says so ("a false REJECT only defers an auto-evolution (safe direction)"). Two adversarial benchmark cases (adv-conflicting-intent-keep-security, adv-security-regression-gap) exercise it end to end in the decision benchmark.

None of the retained rejections is attributed to security-regression-gate. That's not evidence the gate works and not evidence it doesn't. Per-gate attribution was added in !106, and these 10 rows carry no gate name. The evidence for this module is its 6 unit tests and the two benchmark cases.

What's proposed and not built

  • A --gate high default for repositories where deleting files matters. It's a one-word change in CI, but it's a policy decision for each team, not a code fix.
  • Gating unparsed files. Today parsed: false is never a candidate. Failing closed on "I couldn't read the new revision of a file that changed" would close probe row 1, at the cost of blocking every Flow-annotated file in a codebase. Not decided, not implemented.
  • A cross-file call graph. Explicitly not planned: integrate an existing tool rather than build one.

Part 3 — Tests

All counts below come from node --test --test-reporter=tap on 2026-10-12, Node 24.19.0.

tests/unit/mr-report-gradual.test.js — 7 tests, 7 pass

The September audit file. Each test pins one scenario from the table above:

ok 1 - gradual 1a: an import-only MR is already critical and trips the gate
ok 2 - gradual 1b: adding the exec() call to an already-critical file blocks unless that fact is acknowledged
ok 3 - gradual 2: a path acknowledged for process_spawn does not absorb a later eval
ok 4 - gradual 2 (legacy): a bare reason string still accepts the whole path, but the waiver is visible
ok 5 - gradual 2 (control): acknowledgement waives the *first* raise and records the reason and facts
ok 6 - gradual 3 (by design): low→medium then medium→high never trips --gate critical
ok 7 - gradual 4 (declared boundary): the caller of a spawning module is invisible to per-file diffFacts
# tests 7
# pass 7
# fail 0

(Seven, not six. The audit in !104 started with six, and !105 split scenario 2 into the fact-listed ack and the legacy-string ack.)

The core of 1b, the case that used to slip through:

const finding = MrReport.diffFacts({ path: 'runner.js', before: IMPORT_ONLY, after: IMPORT_AND_CALL });

assert.deepEqual(finding.dangerous.added, ['process_spawn']);
// The risk level cannot go above critical, so direction is "unchanged"...
assert.deepEqual(finding.risk, { before: 'critical', after: 'critical', direction: 'unchanged' });

// ...but the gate triggers on the new dangerous fact, not only on direction.
const result = MrReport.report([{ path: 'runner.js', before: IMPORT_ONLY, after: IMPORT_AND_CALL }]);
assert.equal(result.riskRaised.length, 0);
const verdict = MrReport.gate(result, 'critical');
assert.equal(verdict.blocked, true);
assert.ok(MrReport.renderGate(verdict).includes('stays `critical`, new (process_spawn)'));

// A fact-specific acknowledgement waives exactly this capability.
const waivedVerdict = MrReport.gate(result, 'critical', { 'runner.js': { reason: 'runs git', facts: ['process_spawn'] } });
assert.equal(waivedVerdict.blocked, false);

// An acknowledgement of a different capability does not.
assert.equal(MrReport.gate(result, 'critical', { 'runner.js': { reason: 'imports only', facts: ['child_process'] } }).blocked, true);

And scenario 3, which pins a limitation on purpose. If someone "fixes" it by quietly lowering the threshold, this test fails and forces the conversation:

assert.equal(MrReport.gate(mr1, 'critical').blocked, false);
assert.equal(MrReport.gate(mr2, 'critical').blocked, false);

// The same creep is caught by a stricter threshold, which is the documented knob.
assert.equal(MrReport.gate(mr2, 'high').blocked, true);
assert.equal(MrReport.gate(mr1, 'medium').blocked, true);

tests/unit/mr-report.test.js — 13 tests, 13 pass

The original report and gate tests. The gate-specific ones:

ok 9 - gate: blocks only when a file is raised to the threshold or above
ok 10 - gate: a file that was already critical does not block later changes that add no dangerous fact
ok 11 - gate: an acknowledged path is waived with its reason instead of blocking
ok 12 - gate: removing the dangerous operation is never blocked
ok 13 - the report layer is pure: no network, no LLM, no filesystem, no git

Test 10 is the "candle on the table" test, the title of this article in assertion form:

const stillCritical = SPAWNS.replace('module.exports = { run };', 'module.exports = { run, VERSION: 2 };');
const result = MrReport.report([{ path: 'runner.js', before: SPAWNS, after: stillCritical }]);

assert.equal(result.highestRisk, 'critical');
assert.equal(result.riskRaised.length, 0);
assert.deepEqual(result.findings[0].dangerous.added, []);
assert.equal(MrReport.gate(result, 'critical').blocked, false);

The other eight cover the report itself: reverse diffs report removals and lowered risk, added and deleted files, a formatting-only change reports nothing, an unparsable revision reports nothing instead of a false absence, and the same input renders byte-identical output twice.

tests/unit/security-regression-gate.test.js — 6 tests, 6 pass 

ok 1 - rejects dropping a crypto primitive from a security module
ok 2 - rejects removing input validation (fewer throws) on any file
ok 3 - rejects a verification-bypass cache on a keep_security target
ok 4 - allows a patch that ADDS validation (no regression)
ok 5 - allows an unrelated refactor that preserves throws and primitives
ok 6 - no baseline or no new code is never a regression

The whole suite

npm test (node --test tests/*.test.js tests/unit/*.test.js): 639 tests, 10 suites, 639 pass, 0 fail.

Closing

A gate that fires on presence gets muted within a week. A gate that fires on change can stay switched on, because when it fires it's telling you something new. Over Sentinel's whole history, that's 3 merge requests out of 118.

The interesting part of this gate isn't the four-rung ladder. It's how the holes are handled. A reviewer asked a hard question. The answer was written as tests that passed while documenting the failure, and only then did one small change turn two of those tests from "this is broken" into "this is fixed". The remaining holes (slow climbs, cooperating files, unreadable files, eval hidden behind a computed property) are still in the test file and in this article, because a gate whose blind spots are written down is one people can rely on.

articles.title: The "Health Check" of a PCB: From AOI to X-Ray to Functional Test

articles.body_html:
At AnyPCBA, every board goes through a "health check" before it leaves the factory.

This isn't a single step—it's a chain of inspections: AOI, X-Ray, ICT, and FCT. Each one answers the same question: is this board safe to ship?

But many engineers have a fuzzy understanding of this chain. They know the factory "tests it," but not exactly what's tested, what can be caught, and what can't.

This article breaks down the inspection chain, layer by layer: what each test does, what it can catch, and what it can't.

Layer 1: AOI—Visible Defects Don't Stand a Chance

AOI (Automated Optical Inspection) is the first layer of the chain.

The principle is simple: high-resolution cameras capture the PCB surface and compare it against a "golden reference" image to find differences. It inspects visible solder joints and components.

What AOI can catch:

  • Missing or misaligned components: a component that wasn't placed, or placed incorrectly
  • Solder bridges: two pins that shouldn't be connected, connected by solder
  • Insufficient solder or cold joints: weak or insufficient solder joints
  • Tombstoning: a component standing on one end
  • Polarity errors: diodes, capacitors, or ICs placed in the wrong orientation

AOI is fast and high-coverage, well-suited for high-volume inspection. But its limitation is obvious: it can only see the surface.

For BGA and QFN packages, where the solder joints are hidden beneath the package body, AOI is helpless. The joints are under the chip—the camera can't see them.

Layer 2: X-Ray—Seeing Through the Joints
X-Ray inspection exists to solve AOI's blind spot.

X-Ray uses the penetrating power of X-rays to "see through" BGA bottoms, QFN bottoms, and through-hole interiors. It inspects solder joint quality hidden beneath packages.

What X-Ray can catch:

  • BGA voiding: bubbles inside solder balls, affecting mechanical strength and thermal conductivity
  • Solder ball bridging: adjacent balls under a BGA connected together
  • Missing or shifted solder balls: balls that should be there but aren't, or are misaligned
  • Poor via filling: incomplete fill inside vias, affecting reliability
  • QFN bottom joint defects: poor soldering on the thermal pad under the chip

X-Ray's limitation: it can see the "shape" of a solder joint, but it's hard to directly judge "strength" and "electrical performance." A joint that looks normal may actually be a cold joint.

Layer 3: ICT—Checking Electrical Connections

ICT (In-Circuit Test) uses probes to contact test points on the board and measure electrical parameters point by point.

It checks circuit connection integrity and component electrical performance.

What ICT can catch:

  • Opens: connections that should exist but don't
  • Shorts: connections that shouldn't exist but do
  • Component value deviation: actual resistance or capacitance outside spec
  • Component orientation errors: polarized components placed backwards
  • Missing components: components that should be installed but aren't

ICT's core metric is "coverage." Ideally, every electrical net should have a test point. But in reality, high-density boards have limited test point space, and coverage often falls short of 100%. Insufficient test point coverage means some defects may slip through.

Layer 4: FCT—Verifying Function

FCT (Functional Circuit Test) is the last layer—and the closest to "real-world use."

It powers up the board, simulates actual operating conditions, and verifies whether the board functions correctly.

What FCT can catch:

  • Functional abnormalities: a functional module that doesn't work
  • Performance below spec: excessive output noise, insufficient response speed
  • Timing issues: power-up sequencing or signal timing that doesn't meet requirements
  • Boundary condition failures: abnormal operation under extreme temperature or voltage

FCT's key lies in test case design. The more comprehensive the test cases, the more potential problems are caught. If test cases only cover "normal operating conditions," boundary condition issues will be missed.

One Chain, Different Roles, None Optional

Looking at all four inspections together, their roles are clear:


No single inspection is universal. AOI can't see BGA bottoms. X-Ray can't see electrical performance. ICT can't see functional behavior. FCT can't see long-term reliability.

That's why the chain must be complete. Each inspection covers the blind spot of the one before it.

What This Means for Hardware Engineers

1. Test coverage determines recall rate. If you only do AOI, BGA-related defects will slip through. If you only do ICT, functional abnormalities will slip through.

2. Test point design must happen at the design stage. ICT coverage depends on test point accessibility. If test points aren't reachable, even the best ICT equipment is useless.

3. FCT test cases must cover boundary conditions. Testing only "normal operating conditions" isn't enough. Temperature boundaries, voltage boundaries, and timing boundaries are all potential failure points.

4. Understand the boundaries of each inspection. Don't expect any single inspection to "handle everything." The value of the chain lies precisely in each inspection knowing what it can't see.

At AnyPCBA, our inspection chain covers AOI, X-Ray, ICT, and FCT, serving small-to-medium volume PCB and PCBA projects from 5 to 5000 pieces.

Specifically, what we can support includes:

  • Full AOI inspection: every board goes through automated optical inspection before shipment, checking component placement, solder joint quality, and polarity
  • X-Ray inspection: for BGA, QFN, and other hidden-joint packages, providing void rate, bridging, and offset detection
  • ICT testing: based on the customer's test point design, providing in-circuit test fixtures and test programs
  • FCT functional testing: working with customers to define test cases covering normal operating conditions and boundary conditions
  • Test point accessibility review: checking test point layout during DFM review, catching coverage gaps early
  • Test fixture design and fabrication: for small-to-medium volume projects, providing fast, low-cost test fixture solutions

Our manufacturing capabilities cover 2–64 layers, including HDI, rigid-flex, and high-frequency hybrid. We hold ISO 13485 (medical) and IATF 16949 (automotive) certifications. If you're working on a PCB or PCBA project that needs a complete inspection chain, contact us through our website.

What defects have slipped through inspection in your projects? Share your experience in the comments.
